item.title: Directed Evolution of an α-2,3-Sialyltransferase Enables Efficient Sialylation of Glycoproteins
item.description:
Abstract
α-2,3-Sialylation is a key terminal modification of glycans, playing pivotal roles in regulating glycoprotein stability, immune recognition, and glycoengineering. However, some α-2,3-sialyltransferases exhibit undesired side activities and a restricted substrate scope, thereby limiting their application in the modification of complex glycans and therapeutic glycoproteins. Here, we employed a directed evolution strategy integrating ultrahigh-throughput screening with deep mutational scanning (DMS) to engineer CstI from Campylobacter jejuni. This study provides the DMS platform for glycosyltransferases that enabled us to delineate its mutational tolerance landscape across the entire sequence and identify key functional residues. By combining beneficial mutations with a C-terminal truncation, we developed a highly active mutant, designated M8, which demonstrated a sevenfold increase in kcat compared to the wild type. Furthermore, M8 exhibited a markedly broad donor and acceptor substrate scope, achieving quantitative (∼100%) sialylation of oligosaccharides and efficient sialylation of glycoproteins, including bovine asialofetuin and a monoclonal antibody. Importantly, α-2,3-sialylation by M8 prolonged the serum half-life of asialofetuin in mice. Microsecond-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and computational alanine scanning suggested that the enhanced activity is associated with weakened enzyme–product interactions, which may facilitate catalytic turnover. Together, these features make M8 a promising and efficient biocatalytic tool for the sialylation of complex glycans and therapeutic glycoproteins.

item.title: Interfacial Electronic Synergy in Tandem Catalysts Steers C−C Coupling for Selective CO 2 Electroreduction to Ethylene
item.description:
Abstract
Tandem catalysis integrating CO-generating sites with a Cu catalyst represents a promising strategy for converting CO2 into high-value fuels and chemicals. While optimizing *CO availability is a central goal, the influence of adjacent tandem sites on the intrinsic reactivity of Cu remains underexplored. Herein, we report a rationally designed tandem catalyst featuring CuO nanosheets supported on a N-doped carbon matrix anchoring Ni single atoms. Aberration-corrected microscopy reveals the spatial proximity of Ni atoms to the Cu interfaces, ensuring efficient *CO spillover. In situ spectroscopy and theoretical simulations demonstrate a dual functionality, where the Ni single atom sites elevate *CO coverage while concurrently inducing electronic coupling that enriches electrons at the Cu interfaces. This synergistic effect optimizes the adsorption dynamics of key intermediates, effectively lowering the kinetic barrier for C−C coupling. Consequently, the tandem catalyst achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 68.0% and a partial current density of −0.41 A cm−2 for C2H4, representing a 34% enhancement in C2H4 selectivity over pristine CuO. This work underscores the role of interfacial electronic coupling in refining tandem catalysis toward selective multicarbon synthesis.

item.title: Role of 1,3-Dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1H-benzo[d]imidazole (BIH) in the Photo-driven H 2 Production: Hydrogen Atom Transfer vs Stepwise Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer?
item.description:
Abstract
1,3-Dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1H-benzo[d]imidazole (BIH) is widely used as a sacrificial donor in homogeneous photocatalytic reductions and commonly described as a two-electron donor operating through an electron-transfer/proton-transfer/electron-transfer pathway. A recent study proposed instead that BIH activates a NiFe catalyst for hydrogen evolution via hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) from BIH•+, prompting renewed interest in the fundamental reactivity of this key intermediate along with important consequences for its use in CO2 photocatalytic reduction. Here, we re-evaluate the mechanistic interpretation, by analyzing the reported NMR and EPR data, and it appears that a HAT pathway is not unambiguously supported. Using thermodynamic and kinetic data obtained from cyclic voltammetry of BIH, we conduct numerical kinetic simulations to investigate the competition between HAT and PT–ET (proton transfer–electron transfer) pathways. The results indicate that BIH•+ deprotonation is relatively fast, thus preventing efficient HAT. Subsequent BI• oxidation limits its accumulation to transient sub-micromolar concentrations, making its detection under the reported conditions unlikely and therefore invalidating previous assignments; we assign the EPR spectrum to the reduced photosensitizer. A kinetic analysis identifies the key dimensionless parameters governing selectivity and shows that HAT would dominate only with high HAT rate constants (above 107–108 M–1 s–1). Overall, the classical PT–ET mechanism remains consistent with available data.

item.title: Competition between Enthalpy and Entropy in Dynamic Catalysis of Alumina-Supported Pd Nanoclusters
item.description:
Abstract
The catalytic performance of supported metal nanocatalysts is intrinsically linked to their dynamic structural evolution under reaction conditions. However, resolving these rapid, multiscale transitions remains a formidable challenge. Here, we combine an active learning workflow with enhanced sampling molecular dynamics to construct machine-learning potentials to simulate structural dynamics and O2 dissociation on Pd nanoclusters supported on γ-Al2O3 and θ-Al2O3 surfaces. We reveal that strong metal−support interactions significantly alter the phase behavior of Pd clusters: unlike unsupported clusters, which undergo sharp, size-dependent solid−liquid transitions, supported clusters exhibit suppressed fluxionality and lack distinct melting transitions. Despite these structural differences, the free energy of O2 dissociation displays a universal U-shaped temperature dependence across all systems. Thermodynamic decomposition identifies the origin of this profile as competition between enthalpy and entropy that governs the Gibbs free energy: as temperature rises, the enthalpic drive is eventually counterbalanced by an entropic penalty. These findings suggest that the support primarily governs the structural stability and phase behavior of Pd nanoclusters, whereas the intrinsic thermodynamics of O−O bond scission are dictated by the local chemical environment. This work provides atomistic insight into supported nanoparticle catalysis and offers guidance for designing nanocatalysts with improved activity and durability.

item.title: Palladium-Modified Cobalt Oxides for Optimized Interfacial Oxygen Vacancies in Visible-Light FDCA Production
item.description:
Abstract
Selective oxidation of biomass-derived 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) into 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) is a crucial step toward circular production of polyethylene furanoate (PEF). Herein, a reductive defect engineering strategy for Pd-modified cobalt oxides is introduced to enhance photocatalytic FDCA production under visible light. By combining Pd ion incorporation with NaBH4-assisted calcination, abundant surface oxygen vacancies (OV) are created in cobalt oxides during embedded Pd reduction. The optimized photocatalyst achieves >99% HMF conversion and a 69% FDCA yield, with sustained catalytic performance upon reuse. Surface analysis reveals a linear relationship between OV density and photocatalytic activity. As-obtained FDCA is subsequently polymerized with ethylene glycol to produce PEF, providing a proof-of-concept demonstration of coupling visible-light-driven photocatalytic biomass valorization with downstream polymer synthesis.

item.title: Multi-Enzyme Cascade Catalysis: A Route-Centered Framework for Designing Biocatalytic Systems
item.description:
Abstract
Multi-enzyme cascade catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for molecular synthesis by integrating multiple enzymatic transformations into coordinated systems. However, the rational development of increasingly complex cascades remains challenging because route planning, enzyme discovery, cascade implementation, and process optimization are often considered separately. This review presents a route-centered framework in which biocatalytic retrosynthesis, retrobiosynthesis, and computer-assisted pathway design guide the generation and prioritization of candidate routes before enzyme selection. Route evaluation extends beyond reaction plausibility: the selected pathway determines the catalytic functions required, the compatibility among individual steps, and the constraints on implementation. Enzyme discovery and engineering then provide the catalysts needed to realize these functions, including transformations that extend beyond the natural enzymatic repertoire. Cascade architecture and pathway organization are then considered in relation to cofactor requirements, catalytic compatibility, intermediate management, and process constraints, while optimization at the enzyme, pathway, and process levels addresses limitations that emerge during implementation. Future progress will depend on increasingly predictive and data-driven workflows that integrate route design, enzyme properties, pathway interactions, and process development, moving multi-enzyme cascades from empirical assembly toward programmable biocatalytic systems.

item.title: Mechanistic Explanation of Triplet Energy Transfer Reactions Mediated by Transition-Metal-Based Photosensitizers
item.description:
Abstract
This study provides a mechanistic explanation of triplet energy transfer processes mediated by transition-metal-based photosensitizers. Transition-metal-based photosensitizers have recently come to prominence for their ability to generate catalytic systems that display an improved array of reactions. However, there remains little understanding of the exact mechanism by which these photosensitizers activate the catalytic center. The mechanistic aspects of E → Z photocatalyzed isomerization of alkenes in the presence of organic photosensitizers were examined in a previous work using kinetic arguments based on a four-state model. In this work, we show that the four-state model is not suitable for transition-metal-based photosensitizers and, instead, two additional states are required, resulting in a six-state model. In addition, we are able to show how the kinetic properties can be modified to control the rates of excited-state single electron transfer and triplet energy transfer pathways. The developed six-state model thus provides design parameters for developing catalysts that are activated selectively by either triplet energy transfer or single electron transfer.

item.title: Diverse Pathways for Migration in Carbonylation: From Transition-Metal Catalysis to Radical Strategies
item.description:
Abstract
Migratory reactions in carbonylation represent a distinctive and intriguing class of organic transformations, which typically involve the migration of reactive sites and the translocation of functional groups. Accordingly, the precise site-selective regulation of migration reactions is of great academic significance while remaining a formidable synthetic challenge. Furthermore, the promising applications of migratory reactions in energy chemistry and chemical engineering have been increasingly recognized by synthetic chemists. Therefore, this review summarizes the research advances in migratory reactions in carbonylation over the past two decades, classified into two major categories: transition-metal-mediated and radical-mediated pathways. Transition-metal-mediated migratory reactions in carbonylation predominantly rely on ligand engineering to precisely modulate migration regioselectivity, whereas radical-mediated migratory reactions in carbonylation enable functional group translocation at specific reactive sites. These two complementary strategies greatly enrich the methodological diversity of migratory transformations. It should be noted that migratory hydroformylation reactions are not covered in this review.

item.title: Polymerization Induces Catalyst Microenvironment Variations
item.description:
Abstract
How polymer growth reshapes the environments surrounding immobilized catalysts remains poorly characterized; this gap hinders linking microscale catalytic behavior to macroscale reaction outcomes. We introduce an operando fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy method using a polymerizable, viscosity-sensitive BODIPY molecular rotor to probe resin-supported Hoveyda–Grubbs catalysts during ring-opening metathesis polymerizations. Increasing fluorescence lifetimes reveal progressive confinement with spatial heterogeneity at particle and subparticle levels. Thus, nominally identical immobilized catalysts experience different confinement and accessibility during reaction. Distinct temporal responses for cross-linked and noncross-linked polymers demonstrate network-dependent behavior. Together, these measurements characterize how polymerization generates heterogeneous environments around catalysts.

item.title: Second-Sphere Electrostatic Catalysis Drives O−O Bond Activation in 3-Hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-Dioxygenase
item.description:
Abstract
3-Hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (HAO) is a non-heme iron-dependent enzyme that catalyzes oxidative aromatic ring cleavage of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3-HAA), a key step in quinolinic acid formation and de novo NAD+ biosynthesis. Despite extensive structural and kinetic characterization, the molecular origin of O−O bond activation in HAO—and in particular the critical role of the second-sphere residue Arg47—has remained unresolved. Here, quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations delineate the complete reaction pathway and electronic structures of the key intermediates in wild-type HAO and the R47A mutant. The calculations reproduce the experimental activation barriers and account for the >1100-fold loss of activity upon mutation. In contrast to the conserved histidine in the related extradiol dioxygenases HPCD and APD, which promotes O−O cleavage by direct proton transfer, Arg47 acts primarily through electrostatic catalysis. Its positively charged guanidinium group preferentially stabilizes the O−O cleavage transition state and polarizes the Fe−O−O unit, thereby promoting bond scission without direct proton donation. Comparison with non-heme iron dioxygenases further shows that analogous arginine residues perform distinct functions in different non-heme iron dioxygenases. These results identify second-sphere electrostatic stabilization as an alternative strategy for O−O bond activation and highlight how local protein electrostatics can control the reactivity of metal−oxygen intermediates.

item.title: Palladium-Catalyzed Alkene-Relayed Alkylation/Annulation of Aryl Iodides via Multicomponent C–H Activation
item.description:
Abstract
A palladium-catalyzed maleimide-relayed multicomponent C–H alkylation of simple aryl iodides has been developed. This reaction provides a direct and tunable approach to a diverse array of succinimide-fused dihydrophenanthrenes and acenaphthene derivatives via three- or four-component C–H activation cascades with high regioselectivity in moderate to good yields. The practicality of this protocol is demonstrated by its broad substrate scope and good functional group tolerance. Notably, the resulting polycyclic frameworks represent important structural motifs found in numerous biologically active organic molecules.

item.title: Alkylsilyl Peroxide-Enabled Copper-Catalyzed Asymmetric Three-Component Alkylarylation of Vinylarenes with Alkanes and Arylboronic Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Chiral 1,1-diarylalkanes are privileged structural motifs prevalent in numerous biologically active molecules. While radical-mediated alkylarylation provides a powerful route to these frameworks, existing enantioselective protocols typically rely on prefunctionalized precursors, limiting overall atom economy. The direct use of feedstock alkanes via hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) is highly attractive but remains challenging due to the difficulty of balancing radical generation with chiral transition-metal catalysis. Herein, we report an alkylsilyl peroxide-enabled, copper-catalyzed enantioselective three-component radical alkylarylation of vinylarenes with feedstock alkanes and arylboronic acids. The key to this transformation is utilizing t-BuOOTMS as an efficient HAT reagent, enabling alkyl radical generation under mild conditions. Subsequent radical addition and enantioselective arylation governed by a binaphthyl-tethered bisoxazoline ligand provide direct access to diverse enantioenriched 1,1-diarylalkanes in good yields and high stereocontrol.

item.title: Merging Pt-Doped TiO 2 Photocatalysis with Nickel Catalysis Enables Redox-Reagent-Free Decarboxylative C(sp 3 )–C(sp 2 ) Cross-Coupling
item.description:
Abstract
Merging heterogeneous Pt-doped TiO2 photocatalysis with homogeneous nickel catalysis enables redox-reagent-free decarboxylative C(sp3)–C(sp2) cross-coupling of carboxylic acids with (hetero)aryl halides. The dual catalytic system uses the air-stable Ni(0) precatalyst Ni(COD)(DQ) and 2,6-lutidine without an external reductant or oxidant, enabling nickel turnover despite the mismatch in redox potentials between the Pt-doped TiO2 conduction band and the relevant nickel couples. The system accommodates a range of (hetero)aryl halides, and the photocatalyst retains activity across three consecutive runs, including two reuse cycles.

item.title: Lewis Acid-Directed Oxygen-Down Interfacial Water Regulation Stabilizes Local pH for Robust High-Current-Density Propylene Epoxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Propylene oxide (PO) is an important C3 platform chemical, but its industrial production still relies on energy-intensive and environmentally burdensome routes. Electrocatalytic bromine radical-mediated propylene epoxidation provides a promising alternative by coupling renewable electricity with mild reaction conditions; however, its practical implementation is severely limited by the acidification of the anodic microenvironment at industrially relevant current densities. Herein, we report a Cr-doped spinel cobalt oxide catalyst grown on carbon paper (Cr0.5Co2.5O4/CP) for robust bromine radical-mediated PO electrosynthesis. The Lewis acidic Cr sites not only enrich surface hydroxyl species but also induce a highly ordered “O-down” configuration of interfacial water molecules. This specific orientation knits a robust hydrogen-bonded network, which rapidly transfers anodically generated protons via the Grotthuss mechanism, thereby effectively circumventing localized acidification. Benefiting from the stable, locally alkaline microenvironment, the Cr0.5Co2.5O4/CP catalyst achieves an outstanding PO Faradaic efficiency of 83.9% and a production rate of 2.35 mmol h–1 at a high current density of 150 mA cm–2, maintaining exceptional stability over 60 h of cumulative operation in 1 h runs with electrolyte renewal. This work highlights the decisive role of steering interfacial water structures, offering a generalizable framework for high-current anodic organic electrosynthesis.

item.title: Balanced Hydroxyl Binding Enables Productive Oxygen Transfer in Photocatalytic Benzene Hydroxylation
item.description:
Abstract
Photocatalytic aerobic hydroxylation of benzene provides an alternative to the cumene process, yet its phenol yield remains limited. Previous efforts have largely focused on hydroxyl radical generation, while interfacial binding and utilization of hydroxyl species have received less attention. Here, we regulate the interfacial binding and turnover of hydroxyl species by constructing distinct Pd site configurations on WO3. Under 420 nm irradiation in water and static air, PdOx clusters (PdOx/WO3) achieve 72.3% benzene conversion, 60.1% phenol yield, and 83.1% selectivity, with a phenol formation rate of 525.9 μmol g–1 h–1, 1.76 times that of isolated atoms (Pd1/WO3). Notably, Pd1/WO3 exhibits substantially stronger spin-trap-accessible ·OH signals, demonstrating that measurable radical abundance does not predict productive oxygen transfer. Mechanistic experiments indicate a greater contribution from water-associated, hole-driven hydroxyl generation over Pd1/WO3, whereas PdOx/WO3 more effectively couples photogenerated electrons to O2 reduction and peroxide utilization. Spectroscopy and density functional theory reveal asymmetric weak Pd–OH and strong W–OH interactions at Pd1–O–W sites, but intermediate and comparable Pd–OH interactions at neighboring Pd sites. Balanced hydroxyl binding therefore promotes peroxide activation, C–O bond formation, phenol release, and active-site regeneration across the complete catalytic reaction sequence.

item.title: Spatially Decoupled Cu-ZnO Mitigates Water-Acetylene Competitive Adsorption for Selective Acetylene Semihydrogenation
item.description:
Abstract
Conventional strategies for copper-based electrocatalysts focus on increasing active metal dispersion or strengthening interfacial interactions, yet fail to address the intrinsic competition among multiple reactants (e.g., C2H2 and H2O) and (side) products (e.g., active hydrogen) over the same active sites. In contrast to this paradigm, we demonstrate that a spatially decoupled Cu-ZnO architecture enables efficient C2H2 semihydrogenation by spatially separating H2O activation and C2H2 hydrogenation onto distinct moieties. Operando EIS and FTIR results reveal that ZnO preferentially activates H2O to generate reactive hydrogen species, which subsequently migrate to adjacent Cu sites, where adsorbed C2H2 undergoes selective hydrogenation. This spatial separation bypasses the competitive adsorption between *H and *C2H2 on Cu sites, thereby suppressing hydrogen evolution and promoting ethylene formation. Consequently, the Cu-ZnO-decoupled catalyst achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 95.2% for C2H4 at a current density of 200 mA cm–2, with a peak partial current density of 697 mA cm–2 at a current density of 1000 mA cm–2, substantially outperforming its interacted counterpart. This work establishes spatial decoupling as a general strategy to overcome competitive adsorption in electrocatalytic hydrogenation reactions.

item.title: Unraveling the Location-Dependent Roles of C 60 on Cu/SiO 2 for Low-Pressure Hydrogenation of CO 2 -Derived Ethylene Carbonate to Methanol and Ethylene Glycol
item.description:
Abstract
The indirect conversion of CO2 into methanol via renewable CO2-derived cyclic carbonate hydrogenation offers an attractive alternative to direct CO2 hydrogenation by circumventing thermodynamic limitations. However, the requirement for elevated H2 pressures has hindered practical implementation. Herein, we report a Cu/SiO2 catalyst promoted with multilayer [C60] fullerenes that efficiently hydrogenates CO2-derived ethylene carbonate to methanol and ethylene glycol at merely 0.5 MPa H2 and 180 °C. The optimized 15C60-Cu/SiO2 catalyst delivers near-complete conversion with high methanol productivity and stable operation for over 400 h. Mechanistic investigations reveal three spatially distinct C60 configurations with synergistic yet differentiated roles. Interfacial C60 serves as an electron buffer that stabilizes Cu+ via reversible electron transfer, suppresses Cu sintering, and thereby enhances substrate activation and reaction kinetics. Both interfacial and noninterfacial C60 facilitate methanol desorption and reduce its deep decomposition into CO and CO2, improving methanol selectivity. Free C60, physically separated from Cu, may serve as an auxiliary hydrogen reservoir that improves H2 utilization under low-pressure conditions. The cooperative interplay among these three configurations enables efficient cyclic carbonate hydrogenation under mild conditions and extends to a range of CO2-derived cyclic carbonates. This work establishes multilayer fullerene promotion as a viable strategy for simultaneously tuning metal electronic structure and product diffusion in heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: In Situ Spectroscopic Insights into Dynamic Surface Reconstruction of BDD Anodes for Electrochemical Ozone Production
item.description:
Abstract
Boron-doped diamond (BDD) anodes are well-known for their capability to generate ozone during the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), making them relevant for electrochemical ozone production (EOP) and water treatment applications. While lead dioxide (PbO2) anodes catalyze EOP via a characteristic lattice oxygen-mediated mechanism, the substantial structural and compositional distinctions of BDD have long rendered its surface reconstruction behavior and reaction pathways under harsh anodic conditions largely unclear. Herein, by integrating electrochemical analyses, quasi in situ/in situ spectroscopic and microscopic characterizations, and isotope labeling techniques, we systematically elucidate the dynamic surface reconstruction of BDD and its critical role in acidic water oxidation. The applied anodic potential drives continuous oxygenation of surface carbon during reconstruction, which concurrently promotes the dominant OER and the parasitic carbon corrosion reaction. Notably, the oxygenated functionalities formed within the reconstructed carbon layer serve as a bifunctional active phase for both OER and carbon oxidation, enabling the reaction to proceed via a surface oxygen-mediated pathway. This study deepens the mechanistic understanding of OER, EOP, and carbon corrosion processes over single-component BDD anodic catalysts, demonstrating that surface reconstruction is indispensable for transforming the pristine BDD precatalyst into a functionally active catalytic interface.

item.title: Allosteric Remodeling of Conformational Dynamics Enables Engineering of Dual-Mode LanP M1 Proteases
item.description:
Abstract
LanPM1 zinc metallopeptidases are important RiPP maturation proteases that remove leader peptides through sequential endoproteolytic cleavage and aminopeptidase trimming. Inefficient leader-peptide removal can limit the maturation and engineering of RiPP natural products, yet rational strategies for improving both processing modes remain poorly developed. Here, we identify a conserved loop_II/IV-domain IV interaction network that distinguishes LanPM1 proteases from representative canonical M1 aminopeptidases. Using EryP, a model LanPM1 protease from erythreapeptin biosynthesis, we show that broad disruption of this interface compromises catalysis, whereas selective perturbation of specific interface contacts suppresses aminopeptidase activity while accelerating endoproteolytic processing and altering cleavage-site preference. Structural and molecular dynamics analyses further reveal that these mutations remodel the conformational ensemble of EryP toward open-like states that expose an extended peptide-accommodation groove while preserving local amino-terminal peptide recognition at the catalytic center. Guided by this model, we combined mutations from two interdomain regulatory regions to generate EryP variants with enhanced dual-mode processing and improved tolerance toward motif-disrupted and non-cognate leader substrates. These findings establish a strategy for engineering dual-mode LanPM1 proteases through tunable interdomain dynamics.

item.title: Moderate Pressures of H 2 Enhance the Tandem Upcycling of Polyethylene to Alkylbenzenes
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic conversion of waste polyethylene (PE) to value-added alkylbenzenes has the potential to replace anionic surfactants made from petrochemicals with ones made from recycled carbon. PE depolymerization to surfactant-range alkylaromatics and jet fuel-range alkanes proceeds in the presence of a Pt/SiO2–Al2O3 catalyst at ca. 280 °C. Although the reaction does not require added H2, the rate is enhanced significantly when the reaction is conducted under moderate H2 pressure (1–8 bar). The maximum alkylbenzene yield occurs at ca. 4 bar H2, in agreement with thermodynamic predictions. As P(H2) increases, the rate of C–C bond scission increases initially, then decreases at even higher pressures (>7 bar). While alkane hydrocracking by a bifunctional (metal/acid) catalyst is inhibited by H2 due to reduced olefin formation, aromatics outcompete alkanes and olefins for adsorption onto the active sites. A simple microkinetic model reproduces the observed nonmonotonic kinetic behavior. Thus, moderate H2 pressures enhance both rate and selectivity in PE conversion to surfactant-range alkylaromatics. This strategy expands the potential of polymer upcycling, contributing to a more circular use of carbon.

item.title: Substrate Promiscuity of an Acetyltransferase Drives Euphorbia Diterpenoid Diversity in Petty Spurge
item.description:
Abstract
Acylated diterpenoids from Euphorbia species are bioactive natural products with multidrug resistance reversal and anticancer effects. Their biological profiles are strongly shaped by regioselective acylation, yet the enzymatic logic that installs multiple acetyl groups on structurally divergent diterpenoid scaffolds has remained poorly understood. Here, by integrating tissue-specific transcriptomics, phylogenetic analysis, and functional screening, we identify Ep17169 from Euphorbia peplus as a clade 3 BAHD acetyltransferase that accepts both macrocyclic jatrophane and polycyclic ingenane scaffolds as substrates. Biochemical and computational analyses reveal that Ep17169 displays scaffold-dependent regiodivergent acetylation, favoring C7-OH acetylation on a jatrophane substrate while preferentially acetylating the C20-OH of ingenol. Time-course experiments reveal sequential acetylation with position-dependent rates and are consistent with a spontaneous C3-to-C5 acetyl migration within the ingenane framework. Cavity engineering using ingenol (4) as the substrate yields C20-selective monoacetyltransferase variants (N388F and G390F) with WT-comparable activity (31–35% conversion). Its multifaceted activity—dual-scaffold recognition, regiodivergent acetylation, sequential catalysis, and the demonstrated engineerability of its ingenane-binding pocket—makes Ep17169 a promising starting point for the biocatalytic diversification of pharmacologically relevant diterpenoids. Collectively, our findings reveal how distal cavity residues control substrate reorientation to govern the trade-off between catalytic promiscuity and strict regioselectivity, providing a structural design logic that can potentially be explored beyond the Euphorbia system.

item.title: Metal Cation-Free, Acidic CO 2 Electroreduction Enabled by Non-Zero-Valent Metal Centers
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical CO2 reduction conventionally relies on alkali-metal cation-based electrolytes to stabilize the *CO2– intermediate; however, these cations promote salt precipitation and electrode flooding in practical electrolyzers. In addition, the alkaline microenvironment in typical eCO2RR results in severe CO2 crossover. Here, we demonstrate that non-zero-valent metal centers in late-transition-metal-based molecular catalysts and single-atom catalysts can functionally replace alkali-metal cations, enabling efficient CO2-to-CO conversion in a Nafion-based membrane electrode assembly cell operating under pure-water-fed, cation-free, acidic conditions. Using cobalt phthalocyanine with positively charged Co active sites as a model catalyst, a CO Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 84.4% is achieved at 50 mA cm–2 and a cell voltage below 2.5 V, while conventional metal catalysts (e.g., Cu, Ag, and Zn) remain essentially inactive. Increasing the CO2 feed pressure to 10 bar extends stable operation to 100 mA cm–2 with 73.6% FE of CO. Notably, the system exhibits an ultralow CO2 crossover of 0.70% across 25 to 200 mA cm–2, significantly enhancing carbon utilization. Moreover, long-term stability is demonstrated over 365 h of continuous operation at 50 mA cm–2. In situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal barrierless CO2 activation and electrostatic stabilization of *CO2– by the positively charged Co center. These findings highlight non-zero-valent, late-transition-metal single-atom or molecular catalysts as promising platforms for alkali-metal cation-free CO2 electrolysis and a viable pathway toward stable, high-carbon-efficiency CO2 electrolyzers.

item.title: Machine Learning in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Catalysis: Complementary Strengths across Scales
item.description:
Abstract
Machine learning (ML) is now applied across every stage of catalysis research, yet its track record differs sharply between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis. This perspective examines the structural reasons behind this divergence. We argue that homogeneous catalysis offers ML a more favorable setting for experimental optimization: discrete molecular catalysts, well-defined descriptors, precise measurables such as enantioselectivity and yield, and mature high-throughput experimentation (HTE) platforms. Heterogeneous catalysis, by contrast, has proven more successful for computational screening at scale, drawing on massive DFT datasets (>106 relaxations) and established physics-informed frameworks such as adsorption-energy scaling relations. The contrast is one of complementary strengths, not overall quality. The three classical gaps of heterogeneous catalysis (pressure, materials, and complexity) remain the main barriers preventing ML from closing the feedback loop between computation and experiment. We discuss how self-driving laboratories, operando characterization, and foundation models may drive convergence and identify what each field can learn from the other.

item.title: Ancestors of Arylmalonate Decarboxylase Show Increased Activity, Stability, and Stereoselectivity
item.description:
Abstract
Bacterial arylmalonate decarboxylase (AMDase) generates a wide spectrum of α-chiral carboxylic acids in high optical purity, including several non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and chiral building blocks. However, extant AMDase from Bordetella bronchiseptica (BbAMDase) and related enzymes of the same family have three main limitations: (i) low operational and thermal stability, (ii) limited substrate spectrum regarding the size of the smaller substituent on the α-C-atom, and (iii) low stereoselectivity towards α-alkenyl-α-alkyl malonic acids. To address these limitations, we expanded the structural diversity of the AMDase family by ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR). The phylogenetic analysis of the decarboxylase revealed conserved structural in the hydrophobic active-site cavity, a catalytic motif crucial for activity and selectivity. AMDase ancestors showed higher stability, activity, and, in one case, also stereoselectivity than BbAMDase. While variation of amino acids of the hydrophobic pockets had increased activity and expanded substrate scope in previous work, this structural motif was found to be remarkably conserved throughout the reconstructed ancestors. The substrate scope of the ancestors towards a set of arylmalonic and alkenylmalonic acids was very similar to that of BbAMDase. Inversion of the stereoselectivity by switching the catalytic cysteine residues (G74C/C188G, numbering according to BbAMDase) was successful for ancestor N5, but reduced the activity of evolutionary more distant N131. This shows that a direct transfer of mutations between related enzymes might not be possible even if the active site cavities are conserved. Ancestor N131 exhibited a 294-fold improvement in half-life time and a 1.8-fold increased specific activity (25.1 U mg–1) toward 2-methyl-2-phenyl malonate in a preparative scale application. Computational analysis provided a potential explanation for improved stability by an increase in surface Glu side chains, which form a protective hydration shell that enhances solubility and mitigates aggregation. Ancestor N31 formed 2-methyl-but-3-enoic acid from its corresponding malonic acid in high optical purity (99.7% eeR).

item.title: Understanding of Co-N 3 -X 1 (X = N, S, Se, and Te) Moieties for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Controlled synthesis of single-atom catalysts (SACs) with different first coordination shells offers an ideal platform for elucidating structure–performance relationships in SACs. Herein, a series of SACs with a well-defined configuration of Co-N3X1-C (X = N, S, Se, and Te) were synthesized for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Theoretical calculations reveal that the negative value of the integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population for the Co(dz2+ dyz)–O(p) interaction provides a better correlation than the d-band center with the adsorption energy of oxygen species. In situ X-ray absorption near-edge structure analyses indicate that the adsorption of oxygen species on the catalysts is consistent with the calculated OH* adsorption trend. The energy gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital of SACs and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of O2 shows a linear relationship with the Bader charge related to O2 activation. Theoretical calculations and in situ Raman spectroscopy indicate that Co-N3S1-C realizes a better balance of O2 activation and *OH desorption, enabling it to exhibit the optimal catalytic activity with an E1/2 of 0.90 V and the largest turnover frequency value of 21.5 s–1. Furthermore, a liquid zinc-air battery with a Co-N3S1-C cathode delivers a power density of 255.4 mW cm–2, which is higher than that of the battery with a Pt/C + IrO2 cathode (196.6 mW cm–2) and most of the Fe- and Co-based electrocatalysts as cathodes reported in the literature. These findings could shed insight on the theoretical exploration of SACs and the heterogenization of homogeneous catalysts.

item.title: Regio- and Enantioselective Allylboration of 1,3-Dienes
item.description:
Abstract
Despite numerous strategies for 1,3-diene difunctionalization, methods that enable regio- and enantioselective allylation remain underdeveloped. We report a Cu/Pd synergistic catalytic approach for the regio-, enantio- and E-selective allylboration of acyclic 1,3-dienes, delivering chiral allyl boron-containing 1,5-dienes with high selectivity. These products serve as versatile intermediates for downstream transformations, including the synthesis of chiral cyclopentene frameworks bearing multiple stereocenters. This strategy provides streamlined access to valuable building blocks from simple hydrocarbons. Density functional theory (DFT) studies reveal a convergent mechanistic manifold in which multiple productive transmetalation pathways funnel into a common bis(allyl)palladium intermediate. Regio- and E-selectivity are established during the reductive elimination step from this intermediate, whereas the enantioselectivity is likely governed by the copper catalytic cycle.

item.title: Organic Photocatalysis: From Molecular Entities to Dynamic Catalytic Systems
item.description:
Abstract
The activity and performance of organic photocatalysts are commonly rationalized by means of their molecular structures and properties. However, the increasing complexity of modern photocatalytic systems challenges this simplified view. In many photocatalytic processes, the identity, function, and selectivity of the active catalyst are determined by its interactions with the surrounding environment and emerge only under specific operating conditions. Through selected examples, this perspective explores the evolving versatility of organic photocatalysts beyond their conventional roles as molecular light absorbers and/or redox mediators. Particular attention is devoted to systems in which catalyst–substrate interactions, structural transformations, coupling with electrochemical settings, and integration into heterogeneous materials give rise to the catalytically active entity. Here, we illustrate how interactions between organic photocatalysts and their surrounding environment can fundamentally shape their properties, mechanisms, and reactivity. Finally, based on current knowledge, perspectives on the possible future evolution of the field are provided.

item.title: Role of Interfacial Silica in the Local Structure, Strain, and Propane Dehydrogenation Activity of Dispersed Ga 3+ Sites
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the structure of the active sites in supported Ga-based propane dehydrogenation (PDH) catalysts is essential, as the Ga–O coordination environment and the nature of neighboring atoms (e.g., Al or Si from SiO2 or Al2O3 supports) strongly influence the catalytic properties. Here, we prepared Ga3+ sites dispersed on Al2O3 and SiOx-Al2O3 supports using atomic layer deposition, tailoring the thickness of the grown SiOx layer and the acidity at the Ga-SiOx-Al2O3 interface. Comparing the propene selectivity and Ga-normalized propene formation rates of the prepared materials reveals that, for the Al2O3 and SiOx-Al2O3 supports, catalytic activity first decreases as Si content increases, which correlates with a decrease in the relative abundance of weakly Lewis acidic tetracoordinate Ga3+ sites in the local coordination environment with Al3+ atoms ([4]Ga(Al) and [4]Ga(Al/Si) sites), driving the PDH activity of those catalysts. In comparison, a reference catalyst with Ga3+ sites dispersed on SiO2 does not follow the trends observed for the SiOx-Al2O3 supports. Instead, it is more active and features the highest abundance of strongly Lewis acidic tetracoordinate Ga3+ sites in the local coordination environment with Si4+ atoms ([4]Ga(Si) sites), which are proposed to drive its PDH activity. Solid-state 71Ga nuclear magnetic resonance studies at ultrahigh field (28.2 T) highlight that the distorted coordination geometry of [4]Ga(Si) sites is characteristic of the silica support and notably less frequent for dispersed [4]Ga(Al) and [4]Ga(Al/Si) sites on alumina and SiOx-Al2O3.

item.title: Cobalt-Catalyzed Oxygen-Ligand Transfer to Carbon Radicals
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic formation of C–O bonds from carbon-centered radicals remains challenging because most radical oxygenation reactions rely on hydroxyl rebound pathways that are largely restricted to hydroxyl transfer. Here, we report a cobalt/photoredox catalytic system that enables intermolecular oxygen-ligand transfer to carbon radicals. The reaction merges cobalt hydride hydrogen-atom transfer with radical acyloxy migration to generate tertiary radicals that are intercepted by cobalt(III)–oxygen complexes through radical ligand transfer. This strategy enables remote-Markovnikov-selective hydration and hydroetherification of alkenes under mild conditions using hydroxy, alkoxy, and aryloxy nucleophiles. Mechanistic experiments and density functional theory calculations support a catalytic cycle involving cobalt-mediated homolytic substitution at a cobalt–oxygen bond. These findings establish catalytic oxygen-ligand transfer as a general platform for constructing C–O bonds from carbon radicals.

item.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ni(I)–Isocyanide Catalyzed Cross-Coupling Reactions: A Density Functional Theory Study of Reactivity and Selectivity
item.description:
Abstract
Cross-coupling reactions are of fundamental importance in organic and medicinal chemistry due to their ability to construct structurally complex molecules efficiently. Among transition-metal catalysts, nickel, particularly Ni(I) species, has attracted increasing attention because of its low cost, earth abundance, and electronic flexibility. In this study, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to comprehensively investigate the reaction mechanism of Ni(I)-isocyanide catalyzed cross-coupling and to uncover the factors governing the preference for Kumada cross-coupling over undesired homocoupling pathways. Our results reveal the critical role of molecular rotations, a factor that is often overlooked in computational mechanistic studies. We demonstrate that subtle rotational dynamics can significantly influence reaction selectivity by modulating the accessibility and energetics of competing pathways, with a selectivity-determining barrier of 9.0 kcal/mol. In addition, a systematic analysis of steric and electronic descriptors of the key Ni(III) intermediate shows that combining the percent buried volume (%Vbur) and the topological fuzzy Voronoi cells (TFVC) charge on nickel (q(Ni)) in a two-descriptor multilinear regression reproduces the experimental isolated yields of 13 substrates (R2 = 0.853, Q2(LOO) = 0.724), revealing the decisive role of the organic group transferred from the Grignard reagent. Overall, this work establishes molecular rotational effects as an important mechanistic determinant and offers valuable design principles for the development of more efficient and selective nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling processes.

item.title: Cyclopropenimine Ligands: Coordination Chemistry and Catalytic Applications
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclopropenimines (CPIs) are a class of structurally modular, neutral nitrogen donors in which strong electron donation is coupled to charge redistribution and aromatic stabilization within the cyclopropenium framework. This perspective examines the emerging coordination chemistry and catalytic applications of CPI ligands, with emphasis on how their electronic structure underpins diverse bonding interactions with transition metal and main group centers. Structurally characterized transition metal complexes reveal both conventional coordination and unusual four-electron donation from a single imino nitrogen, while complexes of phosphorus and heavier group 14 elements illustrate how CPI–center interactions vary with oxidation state and secondary coordination. The catalytic potential of this ligand class has recently been demonstrated in copper radical chemistry. CPI-supported copper systems enable the activation of challenging tertiary alkyl halides under mild conditions in both intermolecular radical cross-coupling and intramolecular radical cyclization. Mechanistic studies further underscore the importance of matching ligand-controlled redox properties to the requirements of both radical generation and subsequent catalyst turnover. Together, these studies connect the distinctive coordination chemistry of CPI ligands with their emerging catalytic reactivity and highlight opportunities for further ligand design and applications in redox catalysis.

item.title: An Organocatalytic Borrowing Hydrogen Reaction by Flavin Photocatalyst
item.description:
Abstract
Borrowing hydrogen (BH) reactions offer an atom-economical and green pathway to build complex molecules using abundantly available and inexpensive alcohols as alkylating agents. However, major BH catalysts comprise transition metals, employing decorated ligands and require high reaction temperatures. A full BH cycle using an organocatalyst operating under mild reaction conditions attracts significant attention but remains elusive. We surmise that a complete mechanistic switch from the traditional polar and two-electron-mediated hydrogenation/dehydrogenation routes involving a metal hydride would be able to provide a desirable solution. Herein, we show that a riboflavin catalyst, 10-PF, conducts (de)hydrogenation cycles under photochemical conditions, completely relying on a radical pathway. The accessibility of the iminoquinone/iminoquinol, 2e–/2H+ redox couple facilitates an alcohol dehydrogenation event and stores the extruded hydrogen on the catalyst backbone. The hydrogenation of an olefinic intermediate also follows a radical pathway, where the reduction of olefin by the photoexcited, deprotonated catalyst plays an instrumental role. This reduction is in striking contrast to polar metal-hydride-based reduction. The hydrogenation exhibits great regioselectivity as exemplified by precise olefin reduction in an enone system, which can be attributed to the feasibility of the one-electron pathway. In essence, a mechanistic switch to a radical pathway obviates the need of transition-metal hydrides and the high reaction temperature required for (de)hydrogenation cycles in a BH catalytic routine.

item.title: Copper-Catalyzed Atroposelective Hydroaminocarbonylation of Alkynes: Access to Axially Chiral Amides
item.description:
Abstract
Despite significant advances in asymmetric carbonylation, the construction of open-chain axially chiral styrenes remains elusive, primarily due to their high conformational flexibility and inherently low rotational barriers. Here, we present a copper-catalyzed atroposelective hydroaminocarbonylation of internal alkynes that directly accesses axially chiral amides. This transformation employs a copper hydride catalytic system with CO and O-benzoyl hydroxylamines, operating under mild conditions to deliver products with good regio- and enantioselectivity. The reaction demonstrates practical utility, tolerating a range of functional groups and accommodating some bioactive derivatives. Furthermore, thermal studies confirm the low rotational barriers of the resulting amides, underscoring the challenge successfully overcome by this methodology.

item.title: Electropositive Site Engineering via Ordered Intermetallic Electrocatalysts for Hydrogen Evolution: From M 2 P to Zr 2 M 12 P 7 ( M = Ni, Co, Fe)
item.description:
Abstract
Doping and alloying is a common strategy to modify the electronic structures of transition metal phosphide (M–P) electrocatalyst to improve their performance. However, the disorder associated with doping and alloying leads to a distribution of local crystal and electronic structures, thus complicating understanding of structure-property relationships. In turn, ordered ternary A–M–P phases with distinct crystallographic sites for each element represent tunable single-site catalysts given their diversity in compositions and structures. To maximize the effect of the second transition metal, the electropositive A = Zr was considered. Ternary Zr2M12P7 (M = Ni, Co, Fe, space group: P6̅, structure type: Zr2Fe12P7) phases, which are ordered derivatives of M2P = M14P7 structures, were synthesized and characterized. An ordered replacement of 1/7 of M metal with electropositive Zr resulted in modification of the electronic structure of the corresponding phosphides. Zr2Ni12P7 exhibited a substantial enhancement of HER activity in acidic media, requiring η10 overpotential of only 87 mV to generate a current density of –10 mA/cm2. Measured at identical conditions, Ni2P without Zr required an η10 overpotential of 203 mV. Zr2Co12P7 also exhibited lower overpotential than Co2P. For M = Fe, the HER activity of Zr2Fe12P7 and Fe2P were comparable. DFT calculations reveal that HER activity modifications in Zr2M12P7 follow a volcano relationship with respect to the d-band center position. This study demonstrates that electropositive site engineering through ordered Zr incorporation is an effective strategy for tuning the electronic structure and catalytic function of phosphide electrocatalysts. The d-band center emerges as a useful descriptor of HER activity across both binary and ternary phosphides.

item.title: Metal-Dependent Oxygen Evolution at Interfaces Derived from Structure-Matched Iron and Nickel Self-Assembled Monolayers (SAMs)
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the fundamental differences in activity between iron- and nickel-based catalysts in the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) has been complicated by the structural complexity of traditional heterogeneous systems. To disentangle intrinsic metal effects, a series of simple, precisely structurally defined molecular models with controlled coordination environments was prepared and employed in water oxidation catalysis (WOC). Specifically, four mononuclear complexes, [P(mPEG1Py)3M(H2O)3][ClO4]2 and [SP(mPEG1Py)3M(H2O)3][ClO4]2 (M = Fe, Ni), were synthesized using the multifunctional tris-(6-(2-methoxyethoxy)pyridin-2-yl)phosphine ligand (P) and its phosphine sulfide analogue (SP), providing identical primary coordination environments for both metals. The redox-innocent pyridyl framework, polyether side chains, and S/P anchor groups collectively enable the formation of uniform, orientation-controlled self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) on gold electrode surfaces. All complexes were comprehensively characterized using single-crystal X-ray diffraction, 1H nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared (IR) vibrational, ultraviolet-visible (UV–vis) electronic absorption, SQUID magnetization, and CHN elemental analyses, while SAM formation was confirmed by high-resolution XPS, infrared reflection-absorption spectroscopy (IRRAS), and spectroscopic ellipsometry. Electrochemical measurements show that the PNi-derived electrode exhibits a lower overpotential, a smaller Tafel slope, faster apparent charge-transfer kinetics, and a higher O2-evolution rate than the corresponding PFe-derived electrode. Post-electrolysis XPS reveals substantial transformation and depletion of the initially deposited molecular films, indicating that they are structure-matched surface precursors rather than persistent molecular active species.

item.title: Secondary-Shell Phosphorus Engineering of Fe Single-Atom Catalysts for Efficient Electro-Fenton Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Selective oxygen reduction for efficient in situ hydroxyl radical (·OH) generation underpins cathodic heterogeneous electro-Fenton (CHEF) technology but remains challenging because catalysts must simultaneously promote H2O2 generation and its rapid activation. Here, we report a waste-to-catalyst strategy that upcycles lithium extraction slag from spent LiFePO4 batteries into a phosphorus-modulated Fe single-atom catalyst (Fe-PNC). Fe-PNC achieves over 95% tetracycline degradation within 30 min under neutral conditions and exhibits broad applicability toward diverse emerging contaminants. Notably, its normalized rate constant (kN) is 0.36 min–1 m–2 g, which is 3.3-fold that of Fe-NC, demonstrating that secondary-shell P modulation enhances Fe–N4 site utilization. Combined atomic-scale characterization, in situ spectroscopy, electrochemical analyses, and density functional theory calculations demonstrate that phosphorus resides in the secondary coordination shell, electronically modulating isolated FeN4 sites to optimize oxygen activation and promote the apparent three-electron oxygen reduction pathway for efficient ·OH generation. Life cycle assessment further reveals substantially lower environmental impacts than conventional homogeneous electro-Fenton processes by minimizing chemical consumption and eliminating iron-sludge generation. Beyond providing a circular route for valorizing spent LiFePO4 batteries, this work establishes waste-derived secondary-shell coordination engineering as a general strategy for designing effective single-atom catalysts for electrochemical oxidation.

item.title: Strong Metal–Support Interaction in Ag/TiO 2 Breaks the Activity–Selectivity Trade-off in Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Methane
item.description:
Abstract
Photocatalytic oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) is a promising route for the direct conversion of methane into value-added hydrocarbons, yet it is fundamentally limited by the trade-off between methane activation and overoxidation. Herein, we report that the strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) effect in Ag/TiO2 breaks this activity–selectivity trade-off, enabling high-performance continuous-flow OCM. By precisely tailoring the SMSI through careful control of the reduction temperature and the oxide size/facet, the optimized Ag/TiO2-H catalyst delivers a C2+ hydrocarbon production rate of 22.67 μ mol h–1 with 94.5% selectivity, along with stable operation for over 55 h, outperforming most reported semiconductor-based photocatalysts. In situ and time-resolved spectroscopy reveals that defective TiO2–x overlayers trap holes to activate C–H bonds, while metallic Ag acts as an electron sink for oxygen reduction, establishing a dual-site configuration that selectively forms CH3 intermediates and directs the reaction toward C2+ products while suppressing overoxidation. These findings provide valuable insights into photocatalytic OCM, demonstrating how a rationally tuned SMSI can effectively reconcile the inherent trade-off between methane activation and overoxidation.

item.title: Efficient and Low-Impact Enzymatic Glycosylation with Robust Sucrose Synthase Variants
item.description:
Abstract
Glycosyltransferase-driven glycosylation enables environmentally mild synthesis of high-value chemicals, but industrial implementation is constrained by the cost of UDP-glucose. Sucrose synthase (SuSy) offers an attractive route for UDP-glucose recycling, yet inadequate operational stability has limited its use. Here, we report an integrated engineering workflow that overcomes the longstanding trade-off between efficiency and robustness in glycosyl donor recycling enzymes. We engineered GmSuSy wild-type and obtained variants combining supra-wild-type activity (178%) with enhanced thermostability (ΔTmapp = 13.3 °C), solvent tolerance (70% retained activity in 25% DMSO), and a 123-fold longer half-life. The variants achieved estimated theoretical total turnover numbers of up to ∼10 million (60 °C), supporting their industrial relevance. Mechanistic analyses revealed that long-range residue communication networks couple oligomeric interfaces with active sites, shifting conformational populations toward stable, catalytically competent states, while increasing hydrophobic packing and reducing solvent accessibility. This enhanced robustness enabled significant process-level gains, including >90% conversion yields in indoxyl and methyl anthranilate glycosylation. Techno-economic and life-cycle assessments indicate the potential to halve reaction costs and reduce environmental impacts threefold, establishing SuSy robustness as a key lever for industrial glycosylation.

item.title: Cation Effects on the Electro-oxidation of Alcohols Are Not Mediated Solely by Their Interactions with Adsorbed OH
item.description:
Abstract
In this work, we deconvolute the impact of electrolyte cations on the electro-oxidation of glycerol (GOR) on Pt. UV–vis reflectograms reveal that the presence of glycerol inverts and enhances the magnitude of cation effects on Pt oxidation. A cation-dependent glycerol diffusion coefficient was then identified using 1H-DOSY-NMR, evidencing that cation-induced trends in GOR reactivity are not controlled by the rate of diffusion of glycerol to the Pt surface, and that smaller cations interact more strongly with glycerol than larger ones. The rates of partial oxidation of glycerol to adsorbed carbon monoxide (COad) and of COad oxidation, measured as a function of cation identity using time-resolved ATR-SEIRAS, suggest that global cation-induced trends in GOR activity are driven mainly by reaction pathways that do not involve COad. We emphasize though that this conclusion remains supported primarily by indirect evidence and logical exclusion rather than direct observation. In any case, the results presented here imply that interactions between electrolyte cations and adsorbed oxygenated species (AOS) alone cannot explain the cation-induced trends in electrocatalytic behavior observed.

item.title: Chemoselective Denitrification of Nitrate to Molecular Nitrogen Catalyzed by Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules
item.description:
Abstract
The combination of supramolecular chemistry and catalysis is a powerful tool to engender reactions in confined space. Broadly, this combination can also be viewed as a method to functionally mimic redox metalloenzymes. Herein, we have prepared guest–host nanocapsules based on a porous, {MoV60WVI72}, inorganic Keplerate host internally lined with circa 20 imidazole acetate (ImA) ligands as histidine surrogates, {MoV60WVI72-ImA}. This enabled the encapsulation of approximately 10 Cu(II) or Fe(III) guest active sites, yielding M10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA} (M = CuII, FeIII). These compounds were characterized by various NMR techniques and XPS. Interest in electrocatalytic nitrate reduction has been flourishing in recent years, with NH3 as typically the only product under protic conditions via a dissimilatory reduction pathway. The formation of N2 via a denitrification pathway requires N–N bond formation that can be amplified by reactions in confined space. The investigation of electrocatalytic nitrate reduction catalyzed by M10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA} revealed up to a ∼10:1 preference via N–N bond formation, leading to N2O and N2 within the nanocapsule. Cu10⊂{W72Mo60-Im} was more active and at lower potentials compared to Fe10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA}. 15N guest exchange saturation transfer NMR measurements indicate a low population of NO3– within the capsule albeit in fast exchange with the surrounding aqueous solution. Despite this, quantitative yields were observed under optimal conditions. Dissection of the denitrification pathway indicates the formation of N2O and N2 as major observable products. Intermediate NO2– and NO are transient and quickly reduced since their accumulation leads to nanocapsule decomposition. The Keplerate-based guest–host nanocapsules determined chemoselectivity by control of the reaction pathway.

item.title: Decoding C–O versus C–C Bond Selectivity in Nickel–Metallaphotoredox Carboxylic Acid Cross-Couplings
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding how catalytic systems dictate product selectivity is crucial for advancing cross-coupling chemistry. While nickel–photoredox dual catalysis has enabled both C─C and C─O bond formation from carboxylic acids and aryl halides under deceptively similar conditions, the mechanistic origins of this divergence have remained elusive. Here, we combine systematic experimentation with density functional theory (DFT) calculations and electrochemical analysis to uncover the key parameters that govern whether C─C or C─O bonds are formed. We show that the halide identity of the aryl electrophile exerts an influence: iodides strongly favor esterification via a low-barrier reductive elimination pathway, bromides promote decarboxylative C─C coupling, and chlorides, with higher C─O reductive elimination barriers, yield exclusively C─C products. Complementary experiments reveal that both photocatalyst loading and halide additives modulate selectivity, consistent with the computed energy landscapes. Together, these insights explain the divergent reactivity observed under seemingly similar conditions. By demonstrating how subtle changes in halide, photocatalyst, and additives toggle reaction outcomes, our study provides predictive design principles for exploiting carboxylic acids in nickel–photoredox catalysis.

item.title: Atomically Precise Platinum Nanocluster Catalysts for Efficient Hydrogen Production via Methylcyclohexane Dehydrogenation
item.description:
Abstract
In hydrogen storage technologies with liquid organic hydrogen carriers, the development of efficient catalysts for methylcyclohexane dehydrogenation is highly important. In this study, we developed atomically precise platinum nanocluster catalysts supported on Al2O3 (Ptx/Al2O3; x = 17, ∼51). Comprehensive characterization demonstrated that the catalysts remained highly monodisperse and of uniform particle size (0.86 or 1.15 nm) and maintained a cationic electronic state (Ptδ+) even after thermal treatment. The Pt17/Al2O3 and Pt∼51/Al2O3 catalysts exhibited a mass activity up to 7.9 and 8.2 times higher than that of conventional nanoparticle catalysts. Furthermore, by effectively suppressing undesirable cracking pathways at a low operating temperature of 250 °C, the catalyst achieved both high selectivity (byproduct yield < 3%; below the detection limit) and durability. These findings pave the way for practical guidelines in advanced catalyst design.

item.title: Biocatalytic Carboligation As a Versatile Route to (Rare) monosaccharides
item.description:
Abstract
Rare monosaccharides have emerged as valuable building blocks for the chemical manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and food additives. Although numerous biocatalytic strategies have focused on the interconversion of naturally abundant sugars, bottom-up enzymatic synthesis from smaller carbon sources represents an increasingly attractive alternative route that offers high stereochemical control. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the de novo (or bottom-up) enzymatic synthesis of monosaccharides through carbon–carbon bond-forming biocatalysis (i.e., carboligation). We cover aldolases, transaldolases, transketolases, and the recently developed formolases, highlighting their catalytic mechanisms, substrate scopes, stereochemical outcomes, and complementary synthetic capabilities. Representative synthetic routes toward free trioses, tetroses, pentoses, and hexoses (ketoses and aldoses) are systematically and critically analyzed, with attention to reaction efficiency, isolated yields, and cascade integration. Significant developments exploiting engineered enzymes, multi-enzyme cascades, whole-cell systems, and hybrid chemoenzymatic processes are discussed, including strategies that directly valorize abundant platform chemicals (e.g., glycerol) and C1 feedstocks such as formaldehyde and carbon dioxide into structurally diverse carbohydrate scaffolds. By focusing on experimentally validated syntheses in which target monosaccharides have often been isolated and quantitatively characterized, this review identifies the current strengths and limitations of bottom-up biocatalytic approaches. Finally, emerging opportunities in enzyme discovery, protein engineering, and integrated catalytic cascades are highlighted, illustrating how advances in carbon–carbon bond-forming biocatalysis are paving the way toward selective and versatile access to rare monosaccharides.

item.title: Lattice Carbon Cycling Directs Pathway Selection in CO 2 Methanation over Oligo-Ni Supported on Hexagonal Lanthanum Oxycarbonate
item.description:
Abstract
Controlling reaction pathways is a central challenge in heterogeneous catalysis because competing intermediates can lead to divergent reaction outcomes. Here, we introduce lattice carbon cycling, a mechanism in which lattice-bound carbon dynamically exchanges with gaseous CO2 and influences the subsequent evolution of carbon-containing intermediates. Using oligo-Ni supported on hexagonal lanthanum oxycarbonate (h-La2O2CO3) as a model system, isotope-labeling experiments reveal the reversible removal and replenishment of lattice carbon and show that incorporated carbon can subsequently contribute to methane formation. Operando spectroscopy further shows that this dynamic lattice environment favors the formation and hydrogenation of monodentate carbonate intermediates (*m-CO32–) over competing carbonate configurations. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the modeled lattice CO2 vacancy environment reverses the relative energetic preference of the competing carbonate pathways, favoring the monodentate route. These findings establish lattice carbon cycling as a pathway-regulation mechanism and highlight dynamic lattice participation as a means of controlling intermediate evolution in heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: Enantioconvergent Radical Suzuki–Miyaura C(sp 3 )–C(sp 2 ) Cross-Coupling of Racemic Alkylboronic Esters Via Photoredox/Ni Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Alkylboronic pinacol esters (APEs) are highly versatile reagents in asymmetric synthesis; however, their application in enantioconvergent Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling remains challenging because of the inherently stereoretentive nature of conventional concerted transmetalation. Herein, we report a radical strategy that enables the enantioconvergent deborylative C(sp3)–C(sp2) coupling of readily accessible racemic β-Bpin aryl ketones with aryl bromides via photoredox/nickel dual catalysis. Key to the development is the activation of APEs by LiOMe, which promotes the efficient generation of a prochiral radical intermediate under photocatalytic conditions, followed by enantioselective coupling under chiral nickel catalysis. This protocol exhibits broad substrate scope, furnishing diverse chiral β-(hetero)aryl carbonyl frameworks with high enantioselectivity. Mechanistic studies and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support a plausible radical mechanism and elucidate the origin of the observed enantioselectivity.

item.title: Dual Transition-Metal Electrocatalysis for Allylic Fluoroalkylation of Unactivated Alkenes Using Fluoroalkyl Carboxylic Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Allylic fluoroalkylation enables the facile incorporation of medicinally valuable fluoroalkyl motifs into abundant, structurally varied alkenes. Existing strategies, however, predominantly rely on expensive and atom-inefficient fluoroalkylating reagents or stoichiometric redox chemicals for the generation of productive fluoroalkylating intermediates, which severely limit their scalability and practical utility. Here, we report a Fe/Co dual transition-metal electrocatalytic strategy that merges photoelectrochemically driven iron-catalyzed decarboxylation with cobalt-mediated dehydrogenation to achieve allylic C–H fluoroalkylation of unactivated alkenes. Readily accessible fluoroalkyl carboxylic acids serve as the fluoroalkyl sources, without the use of exogenous redox chemicals or the pre-functionalization of fluoroalkyl carboxylic acids. This catalytic system tolerates a wide spectrum of functional groups and smoothly converts unactivated alkenes into synthetically versatile allylic fluoroalkylated products with good efficiency. Its synthetic utility has been demonstrated through the late-stage derivatization of alkenes derived from bioactive molecules.

item.title: Iodine(III)-Enabled Photocatalytic Skeletal Editing of Carbocyclic Amides Via Radical–Polar Crossover
item.description:
Abstract
Skeletal editing enables the direct modification of molecular frameworks through atom insertion, deletion, or replacement. However, catalytic nitrogen insertion into ring-strained C–C bonds remains challenging, particularly for the synthesis of saturated diazacycles from readily available carbocyclic precursors. Here, we report an iodine(III)-enabled photocatalytic strategy for the skeletal editing of carbocyclic amides through a radical–polar crossover pathway. The method enables formal 2N insertion into bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane (BCP) amides, affording 2,3-diazabicyclo[3.1.1]heptanes, a bridge-constrained scaffold with potential as a diazine bioisostere. Tuning the electronic properties of the acetoxybenziodoxole (BI-OAc) additive further enables the synthesis of benzodiazepines, tetrahydropyrazoles, and hexahydropyridazines from different carbocyclic amides. Mechanistic studies, including the isolation of a cyclization intermediate, support a radical–polar crossover pathway in which the BI-OAc additive is proposed to facilitate productive cyclization, while suppressing linear byproduct formation. The method has been demonstrated across 72 substrates, including gram-scale synthesis and late-stage modification of bioactive molecules. It also accommodates carbon-based coupling partners, enabling formal two-carbon insertion for complementary skeletal editing of carbocycles. This strategy provides a direct approach to nitrogen-rich, three-dimensional molecular frameworks.

item.title: Cu-Catalyzed α-C(O)–C Bond Cleavage of Unstrained Ketones: A Divergent Approach to C–N Coupling
item.description:
Abstract
Cleavage of inert carbon–carbon σ bonds and skeletal editing have emerged as prominent research areas in contemporary synthetic chemistry, leading to significant advances in molecular reconstruction. Nevertheless, the regioselective α-C(O)–C bond cleavage/functionalization of unstrained ketones remains a formidable and underdeveloped challenge. Herein, we report a regiodivergent C–N coupling strategy enabled by copper-catalyzed α-C(O)–C cleavage/amidation and sequential α-cleavage/decarboxylative amination or sulfonamidation of unstrained ketones. Under Cu/O2 oxidative conditions, ketones undergo α-C(O)–C bond cleavage/amidation to furnish a broad range of aromatic amides efficiently. In contrast, under Cu/Rh/O2 co-catalytic oxidative conditions, sequential α-cleavage/decarboxylative amination or sulfonamidation of ketones deliver aromatic amine or sulfonamide derivatives selectively. This protocol features a broad substrate scope, accommodating nearly 102 substrates with yields of up to 99%. Diverse product derivatizations further demonstrate the synthetic utility of the method. A series of control experiments supports the involvement of key intermediates and provides the basis for a plausible mechanism for the selective C–C bond cleavage/C–N bond coupling process.

item.title: Incorporation of Iron Vacancies to Synergize Oxygen Vacancies within Hematite for Boosted Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting
item.description:
Abstract
Metal vacancies can reduce the hole effective mass and accelerate hole migration, which makes them promising for improving bulk charge separation in metal oxide photoanodes for photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting. Nevertheless, controllable construction of iron vacancies (VFe) has rarely been realized in hematite (α-Fe2O3), a widely explored photoanode material that suffers from intrinsically poor bulk charge separation because small-polaron hopping creates a significant mobility mismatch between holes and electrons. In this work, oxygen vacancies (VO) and VFe were simultaneously introduced into α-Fe2O3 in one step via a facile chelator-assisted solvothermal method. In the resulting photoanode, the two types of vacancies act on electrons and holes, respectively, and work synergistically: VO enhance electron conduction by increasing the charge carrier density, while VFe further improve hole transport by reducing the calculated hole effective mass from 5.568 m0 to 3.717 m0, where m0 denotes the free electron mass. Both types of vacancies modulate the electronic structure of the Fe active sites, resulting in an upshift of the d-band center and accelerating the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). This dual-vacancy strategy gives the α-Fe2–xO3–y photoanode with a 3.5-fold enhancement in photocurrent density (1.83 vs 0.52 mA·cm–2 at 1.23 V vs RHE) and an increase in bulk charge separation efficiency from 9.23% to 24.4% compared with pristine α-Fe2O3. After depositing a Co, Fe-nitrilotris (methylene phosphonic acid) (Co, Fe-NTMP) metal–organic cocatalyst, the resulting α-Fe2–xO3–y/Co, Fe-NTMP photoanode achieves a photocurrent density of 2.12 mA·cm–2. This work provides a synthetic strategy and design principles for constructing dual-vacancy configurations in other functional materials.

item.title: Residue-Specific Determinants of CO 2 Reduction in a Tungsten-Containing Formate Dehydrogenase
item.description:
Abstract
Metal-dependent formate dehydrogenases catalyze the reversible interconversion of CO2 and formate with high efficiency, yet their catalytic mechanism remains the subject of active debate, highlighting the need for studies that better define the role of individual residues. Previous mutational studies have focused mainly on formate oxidation, while the contribution of specific residues to CO2 reduction remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated conserved second-sphere and active-site residues in the tungsten-containing FdhAB from Nitratidesulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough to determine how they shape CO2 reduction and contribute to the catalytic mechanism. Variants of four conserved positions (His193, Arg441, Gln409, and Gln890) were generated by site-directed mutagenesis and characterized by steady-state kinetics, EPR spectroscopy, and X-ray crystallography. The mutations produced disparate effects on CO2 reduction and formate oxidation, and structural analysis was essential for interpreting how each substitution perturbed the active-site environment. Only Arg441 is required for efficient turnover in both directions, stabilizing metal coordination and orienting the substrate. His193 contributes to proton transfer and substrate affinity and is only essential for CO2 reduction, revealing a more critical role in this direction. Gln890 and Gln409 modulate catalysis and enzyme activation, underscoring how pterin–protein interactions and precise active site geometry tune reactivity. Together, these findings assign distinct mechanistic roles to second-sphere residues in Mo/W-Fdh catalysis and support a hydride-transfer mechanism in which substrates bind within the second coordination sphere.

item.title: A Lanthanide-Containing PQQ-Dependent Enzyme with Broad Substrate Scope for Sugars, Alcohols, and Aldehydes
item.description:
Abstract
Since the discovery of lanthanide-containing methanol dehydrogenases (Ln-MDHs), lanthanide (Ln) biochemistry has undergone a notable shift, revealing a class of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent oxidoreductases that specifically utilize Ln ions (Ln3+) as cofactors. A few Ln-containing alcohol dehydrogenases have been reported to oxidize a broad range of substrates, including primary and secondary alcohols as well as aldehydes. This suggests the existence of enzymes with broader substrate scopes than previously anticipated. Nevertheless, the number of Ln-containing enzymes that have been biochemically characterized remains limited. Here, we report the discovery and characterization of an Ln-containing PQQ-dependent dehydrogenase from Paradevosia tibetensis, designated sugar-alcohol-aldehyde dehydrogenase (SAA-DH), that unites high turnover with a broad substrate scope spanning sugars, alcohols, and aldehydes. Recombinant SAA-DH was purified in apo-form and reconstituted with PQQ and Ln3+. The enzyme exhibited a dependence on the Ln3+ species, showing maximal activity with La3+ and progressively decreasing activity with heavier Lns, a profile different from reports in which activity peaks around Pr3+/Nd3+. Structural modeling indicates that the absence of the conserved vicinal disulfide and the lack of a tryptophan “lid” generate an expanded, open active site accommodating bulkier substrates. SAA-DH oxidized d-glucose and d-fucose with turnover rates (kcat) of 1241 ± 13 and 1437 ± 11 s–1, respectively. Product analysis of d-glucose confirmed oxidation of the aldehyde group. SAA-DH also efficiently oxidized C4–C5 alcohols and their corresponding aldehydes. Notably, it also oxidized 5-(hydroxymethyl)furfural, pointing to potential use in biocatalytic biomass conversion. Collectively, SAA-DH has substrate promiscuity, high catalytic turnover, and La3+-biased metal preference, thereby expanding the catalytic landscape of Ln-containing enzymes and providing mechanistic insights into Ln biochemistry.

item.title: Electrocatalytic Conversion of Diethylene Glycol into Diglycolic Acid by Promoted Ni 2+ /Ni 3+ Redox
item.description:
Abstract
Diethylene glycol (DEG), a major byproduct generated during industrial ethylene glycol synthesis via ethylene route, possesses potential for value upgrading. Herein, an electrocatalytic conversion route of DEG to diglycolic acid (DGA) has been demonstrated and the reaction mechanism has been explored in-depth. Typically, a Cr-Ni(OH)2/NF (Ni foam) electrocatalyst was synthesized, achieving a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 90.88% and a selectivity of 90.73% in three-electrode configuration.
