Moreover, it also exhibits high FE and selectivity around 90% during a long-term stability test up to 720 hours in a flow cell. Experimental results confirm that Cr doping facilitates the conversion of Ni2+ to Ni3+ and the spontaneous chemical reaction between Ni3+ and the substrate, thereby promoting the Ni2+/Ni3+ redox cycle. Accordingly, the maximum productivity reaches 1481.5 μmol h–1 cm–2, much higher than that of pristine Ni(OH)2/NF. Preliminary techno-economic analysis reveals that the system can offer a profit of 1775 USD ton–1 at 100 mA cm–2, providing certain references for evaluating the economic prospects of the electrocatalytic process. This study provides a pathway for the conversion of industrial diol by-products and the synthesis of important carboxylic acids.

item.title: Evolution-Guided Engineering of a Process-Compatible Thymidine Phosphorylase for the Scalable Cascade Biosynthesis of 2′/3′-Functionalized Purine Nucleoside Analogs
item.description:
Abstract
2′/3′-Functionalized nucleoside analogs are valuable therapeutic agents and essential building blocks for nucleic acid-based medicines; however, their scalable biocatalytic synthesis remains challenging due to insufficient enzyme robustness under process-relevant conditions. Here, we developed an ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)-guided engineering strategy integrated with kcat/Km-based virtual screening to generate a process-compatible thymidine phosphorylase (TP) variant for scalable nucleoside biosynthesis. Among the reconstructed candidates, ASR114 exhibited an optimal balance between soluble expression, catalytic efficiency, and thermostability, displaying an apparent half-life of > 386 h at 50 °C compared with 7.7 h for wild-type EcTP. Biochemical characterization demonstrated that ASR114 enhanced catalytic efficiency toward multiple 2′/3′-functionalized pyrimidine nucleoside donors, with up to a 5.4-fold improvement in kcat/Km values. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that the enhanced catalytic performance of ASR114 was associated with reduced structural flexibility, optimized substrate interactions, and alleviated conformational strain during substrate recognition. By integrating ASR114, EcPNP, and EcADA into a multienzyme cascade system, we established a crude enzyme-based platform for the synthesis of diverse 2′/3′-functionalized purine nucleoside analogs. The optimized process was successfully scaled to 120 L, enabling kilogram-scale synthesis of eight nucleoside analogs with isolated yields of up to 80.3%. This study establishes an evolution-guided framework for engineering process-compatible biocatalysts by integrating ancestral enzyme engineering, computational prioritization, and process-oriented biocatalysis for the scalable synthesis of complex nucleoside analogs.

item.title: Molecular Origins of Negative Catalysis in Synthetic CO 2 Fixation Cycles
item.description:
Abstract
Crotonyl-CoA carboxylase/reductase (Ccr) is among the fastest known CO2-fixing enzymes and is a key catalyst in the design of synthetic CO2 fixation pathways. Ccr catalyzes the reductive carboxylation of enoyl-CoA esters via a reactive enolate intermediate to build the products after CO2 addition. In the absence of CO2, the enolate can be covalently trapped transiently as a noninhibitory C2 adduct, which enhances the catalytic efficiency of carboxylation by suppressing competing side reactions. Notably, enolate reactivity and adduct formation are tightly controlled in the active site of Ccr through negative catalytic strategies: a conserved active site residue (T209) prevents the formation of an alternative inhibitory C4 adduct. The mechanistic basis of this negative catalysis, however, remains unclear. Here, we combine molecular dynamics, QM/MM free energy simulations, and kinetic isotope effects to dissect how Ccr controls competing adduct formation pathways. Simulations show that a single T209V mutation disrupts the active site hydrogen bond network and increases NADPH conformational flexibility, reshaping the free energy landscape to favor C4 adduct formation. Electric field analyses reveal stronger transition state electrostatic stabilization of hydride transfer in wild-type Ccr than in T209V, highlighting electrostatic preorganization as a major contributor to Ccr efficiency. Finally, for the alternative substrate acrylyl-CoA, a central intermediate in synthetic CO2 fixation cycles, computed barriers and isotope effects support a predominant C2 adduct pathway, indicating that pathway selection is largely dictated by substrate chemistry. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework for negative catalysis in Ccr and point to strategies for engineering more robust carboxylases for artificial CO2 fixation cycles.

item.title: A Nanoscale Valley Sink Governs Temperature-Dependent Catalytic Selectivity on Corrugated Iron Carbide
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting reaction selectivity on corrugated catalytic interfaces remains a major challenge when observed pathway bifurcations cannot be rationalized by static, single-site activation barriers alone. Here, by coupling neural-network-accelerated gas–solid nanoreactor molecular dynamics (GS-NMD) with first-principles calculations and microkinetic modeling, we elucidate the atomistic origin of the temperature-dependent ethylene polymerization switch on corrugated Fe3C(102). We demonstrate that product divergence is dictated by the spatiotemporal clearance of dissociated hydrogen adatoms rather than intrinsic C–C coupling barriers. The corrugated carbide surface functions as a spatially coupled nanoscale tandem architecture, wherein exposed top-layer Fe ridges drive primary C–C and C–H transformations, while adjacent subsurface valleys serve as kinetically accessible hydrogen reservoirs. This dynamic framework quantitatively captures key scanning tunneling microscopy observables, including the shift from boundary-confined direct insertion to terrace-wide dehydrogenative oligomerization, simulated apparent intermediate heights, and distinct chain morphologies. Mechanistically, sluggish low-temperature H migration causes local ridge autopoisoning, suppressing C–C coupling and enforcing direct coupling of intact monomers. At elevated temperatures, dynamic adsorbate fluctuations open a facile drainage pathway into the valley sink, continuously evacuating ridge sites to sustain dehydrogenation. These results highlight the indispensable role of multisite byproduct transport across surface topography, offering a generalizable strategy to model and design complex heterogeneous catalysts beyond static single-ensemble descriptors.

item.title: Rewriting Copper-Catalyzed ATRA Reactions through a Cu(II)/Cu(III) Pathway
item.description:
Abstract
Atom transfer radical addition (ATRA) reactions are typically mediated by photocatalytic Cu(I)/Cu(II) redox cycles, whereas Cu(II) complexes generally serve as precursors to the catalytically active Cu(I) species. Herein, we report a Cu(II) complex supported by the rigid tridentate ligand 3,6-di-tert-butyl-1,8-di(pyridin-2-yl)-9H-carbazole (dpc) that displays an unexpected photocatalytic reactivity. While [Cu(dpc)OAc] exhibits low or no activity in established Cu(II)-mediated transformations, it efficiently catalyzes ATRA reactions, such as the chlorosulfonylation of alkenes, that are typical for Cu(I). Electrochemical and spectroscopic studies revealed that the rigid ligand framework suppresses conventional Cu(II)/Cu(I) photochemistry, instead enabling a Cu(II)/Cu(III) photocycle. Mechanistic investigations support the preassembly of a photoactive Cu(II)-sulfonyl chloride complex followed by light-induced radical generation and Cu(III)-mediated product formation. These findings establish a strategy for promoting ATRA reactivity through Cu(II)/Cu(III) catalysis and underline ligand design as a tool for controlling copper photochemistry.

item.title: Diastereoselective Alkylation of Tryptophan and Tryptophan-Containing Peptides via Cooperative Rh(II)/Chiral Phosphoric Acid Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
A cooperative Rh(II)/chiral phosphoric acid (CPA) catalytic system enables highly diastereoselective alkylation of tryptophan derivatives and Trp-containing peptides at both the N(1) and C(6) positions. The reaction exhibits substrate-controlled regioselectivity: unmodified tryptophan derivatives undergo N(1)-alkylation, whereas preinstallation of a phenyl directing group at C(2) switches the selectivity to C(6)-alkylation, with both modes proceeding with high stereocontrol (up to 99:1 dr). The reaction features mild conditions, low catalyst loading, and broad substrate tolerance, enables the late-stage N(1)-alkylation of di-, tri-, and tetrapeptides containing non-nucleophilic residues and the late-stage C(6)-alkylation of di- and tripeptides containing non-nucleophilic residues. Mechanistic studies support a plausible Rh/CPA cooperative catalytic cycle, with CPA-promoted keto–enol tautomerization proposed to govern stereoselectivity.

item.title: Transannular Sigmatropic Rearrangement of Transient Spirocyclic C3 Ammonium Ylides: Stereospecific Access to Bridged Bicyclic Benzo[ b ]azepine Derivatives and Higher Homologues
item.description:
Abstract
We report a stereospecific entry to bicyclic benzo[b]azepines enabled by an unusual sigmatropic [1,5] carbon shift from a transient spirocyclic C3 ammonium enolate. Enantiopure aziridine-substituted chalcones undergo efficient ring expansion to deliver a broad set of benzo[b]azepin-6-ones in consistently high yields with complete transfer of stereochemical information. The strategy is generalized to larger-ring congeners, providing streamlined access to benzo[b]azocines and benzo[b,g]azecines. Mechanistic insight from density functional theory calculations, complemented by natural bond analysis and local energy decomposition, identifies a counterintuitive origin of reactivity: the stabilization of the rate-determining transition state arises predominantly from correlation energy together with geometric relaxation of the dihydroquinoline framework, rather than from strain-release.

item.title: Location-Dependent Phase Evolution of Nickel in Fe 2 O 3 @LaFeO 3 Oxygen Carriers for Chemical Looping Hydrogen Production
item.description:
Abstract
Fe2O3@LaFeO3 core@shell oxygen carriers with controlled Ni incorporation were investigated for chemical looping hydrogen production. The catalytic behavior strongly depended on the initial location of Ni, which led to distinct Ni-containing phases and different structural evolution during redox cycling. The shell-incorporated Ni carrier exhibited stable redox cycling over 100 cycles, whereas the Ni-free and core-incorporated Ni samples showed lower activity or gradual performance decline. Post-cycling characterization suggests that shell-incorporated Ni undergoes redistribution toward Fe-containing regions, accompanied by the formation of a NiFe2O4 phase. DFT calculations provide thermodynamic insight into CH4 dissociation and oxygen-vacancy segregation and migration energetics over relevant oxide phases. These results indicate that Ni location-dependent phase evolution is closely associated with redox stability and catalytic behavior in Fe2O3@LaFeO3-based oxygen carriers.

item.title: Heteronuclear Ru–Fe Dual Single-Atom Sites Anchored on Lanthanum Metal–Organic Framework Catalyzing the Base-Free Selective Oxidation of 5-Hydroxymethylfurfural
item.description:
Abstract
Heteronuclear dual-single-atom catalysts featuring tailorable electronic structures and cooperative dual-site functionalities have received significant attention. However, their applications in the complex selective conversion of biomass molecules are still scarce and challenging. Here, a lanthanum metal–organic framework (MOF)-anchored RuFe heteronuclear dual-single-atom catalyst (RuFe/LaMOF) was prepared. The developed catalyst enabled the base-free aerobic oxidation of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) in water, achieving nearly 99% FDCA yield at 140 °C under 10 bar O2. The incorporation of an Fe promotor to Ru was shown to induce electron interaction probably through the framework oxygen bridge. The proposed Ru–O–Fe motifs allowed possible charge redistribution involving the LaMOF framework, giving rise to electron-rich Ru and Fe dual sites. Such an electronic structure strengthened the adsorption and activation of the substrate and O2 on Ru-dominated active sites promoted by the adjacent Fe sites. Specifically, Fe sites can facilitate O2 activation into selective and reactive ·O2– species, while Ru sites enabled the adsorption and stepwise oxidation of HMF, DFF, and FFCA into FDCA in a more efficient way. As a result, the RuFe/LaMOF catalyst showed a high intrinsic turnover frequency (TOF) of 52.9 h–1 and an initial FDCA formation rate (finitial) of 1.18 mmolFDCA molRu–1 s–1, comparing favorably with the state-of-the-art supported-Ru catalysts. To the best of our knowledge, this work succeeded in synthesizing an LaMOF-anchored heteronuclear dual-single-atom catalyst for the selective transformation of biomass platform molecules.

item.title: Tailoring CeO x /Cu Synergistic Interface for Ampere-Level CO 2 -to-Ethanol Conversion via Cu Penetration Electrode
item.description:
Abstract
The adsorption of the *CO intermediate and the dissociation of H2O are of crucial significance for synergistically facilitating *CO intermediate hydrogenation and thereby triggering *CO–*CHO asymmetric C–C coupling during CO2 electroreduction. However, achieving the controllable construction of synergistic active sites and their quantitative characterization remains challenging. Herein, a CeOx/Cu hollow-fiber penetration electrode (Ce/Cu HPE) with a stable high ratio of Cu+/Cu0 was presented, where CeO2 was employed to regulate the ratio of Cu+ to Cu0 active sites and simultaneously construct a synergistic oxide–metal interface to facilitate the coordination between *CO intermediate adsorption and H2O dissociation. A Faradaic efficiency of 61.2% for CO2 conversion to ethanol and an ethanol current density of 1.35 A cm–2 were achieved at –0.95 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode, corresponding to a 32% ethanol cathodic energy efficiency, and the electrolysis could persist for 200 h in a neutral electrolyte. Integrated spectroscopy and computational analyses revealed a dual-site synergy mechanism: Cu+ sites chemisorb the *CO intermediate, while adjacent Ov–Ce3+ sites dissociatively activate H2O to generate *H; *H spillovers to Cu+ sites, forming *CHO intermediate that induces asymmetric coupling between *CO and *CHO for high-efficiency ethanol formation at the CeOx/Cu interface.

item.title: Microkinetic Modelling of Photocatalytic Water Splitting With Coupled Light Intensity and Temperature Effects
item.description:
Abstract
This work establishes a density functional theory (DFT)-informed microkinetic model to describe light-driven water splitting as a function of temperature and light intensity by integrating DFT calculations with experimental validation. Using Rh/Cr2O3-CoOOH/Al:SrTiO3 as a representative photocatalytic system, the model captures the surface kinetics of water oxidation on the CoOOH (110) cocatalyst surface, while proton reduction and the subsequent recombination of hydrogen radicals are assumed to occur on the Rh cocatalyst. The proposed reaction mechanism exhibits low activation barriers of 0.13 and 0.06 eV for water splitting steps 1 and 3, respectively. Step 2 has a moderate activation barrier of 0.27 eV. In contrast, step 4 is kinetically less favorable and requires a rearrangement of O* and OH·* surface species, exhibiting a Gibbs free energy barrier of 0.93 eV. The formed O2 desorbs from the surface with an activation barrier of 0.73 eV. The microkinetic model incorporating DFT-derived energies showed good agreement with experimental hydrogen production data. Surface coverages of 2H2O* and OH·* were found to be inversely proportional under all investigated reaction conditions. H2 production rates increase with both light intensity and temperature. Degree of rate control analysis revealed that the elementary steps involving the photogenerated charge carriers control the overall rate of the process. These findings represent a microkinetic description of the photocatalytic water splitting mechanism that explicitly incorporates the coupled effects of temperature and light intensity, offering mechanistic insights into the interplay between charge-carrier dynamics and surface reaction kinetics.

item.title: A Highly Active and Promiscuous Esterase for Amide Bond Synthesis under Aqueous Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
A growing number of hydrolase enzymes show acyltransferase activity under aqueous conditions. However, the competing hydrolysis reaction and the limited catalytic rates for these enzymes prevent them from being routinely used for synthetic applications. To find improved enzymes, we generated an enzyme panel based on promiscuous acyltransferase template enzymes. We identified SoEst12, a highly active and selective enzyme belonging to the family VIII carboxylesterases. Kinetics show that this enzyme is up to 8600× faster (kcatapp) than the well-studied PestE using a model reaction for amidation and that its impressive activity is not limited to the model ester. Enzyme loading studies coupled with the kinetics showed a kinetically controlled selectivity for amidation over hydrolysis, which can be best exploited when using a low enzyme loading. SoEst12 displays a wide amine substrate scope with no hydrolysis of the amide product formed. Competing hydrolysis with some of the ester substrates has been reduced by the introduction of a point mutation in the family-conserved WGG motif. Modeling of these point mutants showed that the reduced hydrolysis activity is correlated with an improved affinity for the amine. The SoEst12 crystal structure was solved, and the N-terminus of a cleaved tag of a symmetry neighbor was found inserted into the active site of the enzyme close to a bound acetate, suggesting a “cleaved amide” and giving mechanistic insight into the high activity and selectivity shown by SoEst12. We demonstrate the synthetic potential of SoEst12 by synthesizing the antiarrhythmic drug procainamide and an AKT inhibitor intermediate in buffer using a low biocatalyst loading.

item.title: Copper-Catalyzed α-C–H Cyanation of Amides via Sequential Electron Transfer/Hydrogen Atom Transfer (ET/HAT)
item.description:
Abstract
Cyanated amides, α-cyano amides and α-amino nitriles, are highly desirable motifs and valuable synthons owing to their important roles in chemical synthesis and medicinal chemistry. Conventional approaches to these compounds typically rely on the nucleophilic attack of cyanide on imines (iminium ions) or on radical transformations from prefunctionalized alkyl halides, respectively. Herein, we report a ligand-free, copper-catalyzed cyanation reaction that enables the preparation of both classes of compounds via direct C−H functionalization without light. This method harnesses the strongly reducing carbon dioxide radical anion, aryl-radical-mediated intramolecular 1,5-HAT, and Cu-catalyzed aliphatic cyanation, featuring an efficient sequence of ET/HAT events. The reaction operates simply under mild conditions, employs inexpensive commercial reagents, exhibits broad functional group compatibility and can be applied to functionalize natural products and bioactive molecules with good yields.

item.title: Secondary Sphere Modification Tunes C–OH Bond Cleavage and Redistributes Rate Control in Electrocatalytic CO 2 Reduction by Molecular Cr Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Mitigating the contribution of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions to global climate change has motivated the development of earth-abundant transition-metal catalysts capable of electrochemically reducing CO2 to value-added chemical products. It has previously been demonstrated that bipyridine-based CrN2O2 complexes can selectively reduce CO2 to carbon monoxide (CO) under electrochemical conditions. To improve the kinetic parameters (turnover frequency) of this catalyst family, the effect of adding –OMe pendent substituents to the bipyridine backbone of the ligand structure was explored. Here, two catalysts bearing different numbers and positions of –OMe pendent groups are reported and analyzed with respect to their impact on the proton-transfer step that accompanies C–OH bond cleavage as a part of the catalytic cycle for CO2 reduction. Combining the observed isotope effect for each catalyst with an intrinsic value computed for that catalyst resolves the contributions of CO2 binding and C–OH bond cleavage to rate control individually, giving varying degrees of rate control for CO2 binding across the series. Separating the underlying rate constants shows that, across the series, the rate constant for C–OH cleavage varies by about two orders of magnitude, whereas that for CO2 binding varies by less than a factor of two. This work suggests that the addition of –OMe groups can provide a kinetic enhancement compared to complexes without the substituents; however, the benefit is tempered by shared rate control with the CO2 binding step of the reaction, which was previously shown to contribute to the observed rate.

item.title: The Oxygen Reduction Reaction over Pt Nanoparticles Studied with First-Principles-Based Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations
item.description:
Abstract
The oxygen reduction reaction is essential to reduce the dependence on fossil fuels. Although widely studied, the underlying reason for the onset overpotential of the reaction over Pt-based nanoparticles remains debated. Here, a first-principles-based kinetic Monte Carlo framework is developed to elucidate the main reaction mechanism, rate-determining steps, and the reason for the overpotential. Effects of the aqueous environment with directional hydrogen bonds are incorporated in the kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, and a framework for simulating linear sweep voltammetry is presented. We find that the overpotential originates from the high coverages of oxygen species (*O, *OH, and *H2O), which block sites for O2 adsorption. The kinetic simulations demonstrate that the effects of site-blocking can be tuned by the shape and size of the Pt nanoparticles. The lowest overpotential is obtained for particles in the size range between 3 and 6 nm with large fractions of (111) facets. The developed methods are general and facilitate the understanding and optimization of catalysts used in a range of electrochemical reactions.

item.title: An Alternative Superoxide-Mediated Pathway for Flavin-Dependent Oxidative Dechlorination in HcbA1
item.description:
Abstract
Flavin-dependent monooxygenases typically activate molecular oxygen through flavin-peroxide intermediates. In HcbA1, however, aerobic oxidative dechlorination of hexachlorobenzene (HCB) is accompanied by the formation of flavin-N5-oxide (FlN5O), raising the question of how oxygen activation is coupled to substrate dechlorination and oxidation. Here, we use multiscale computational approaches, including structural analysis, molecular dynamics simulations, density functional theory, and QM/MM calculations, to evaluate the feasibility of an alternative superoxide-mediated pathway. The calculations support a mechanistically plausible sequence in which superoxide generated from reduced flavin reacts directly with HCB prior to flavin-peroxide formation. Protein-free DFT calculations indicate that the proposed radical chemistry is intrinsically feasible, while QM/MM calculations show that the key transformations are compatible with the structural and electrostatic environment of the HcbA1 active site. Comparison with canonical flavin-peroxide pathways further indicates that the active-site architecture preferentially pre-organizes the reactants for the proposed direct superoxide pathway, although the present calculations do not exclude the involvement of the flavin-peroxide intermediate. Together, these results support direct superoxide reactivity as a plausible alternative mode of oxygen activation in HcbA1 and provide experimentally testable hypotheses for understanding pathway selection in flavin-dependent catalysis.

item.title: Cross-Selective Alkyl–Alkyl Negishi Coupling at Isolable, High-Spin ( S = 3/2) Cobalt(II)–Alkyl Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
A high-spin (S = 3/2) cobalt(II)–dialkyl complex supported by the weak-field ligand N,N,N’,N’-tetramethylethylenediamine (TMEDA) served as a precatalyst for alkyl–alkyl Negishi cross-coupling of alkyl bromide electrophiles. Organometallic studies indicated the isolability of the cross-coupling resting state (TMEDA)cobalt(II)–monoalkyl bromide complex, which was resistant against deleterious β-hydride elimination due to the high-spin (S = 3/2) electronic configuration disfavoring β-agostic H-to-Co interactions. During catalytic cross-coupling, kinetic studies indicated rate-determining formation of cobalt(II)–dialkyl, which was kinetically competent for bromine atom abstraction of bromocyclohexane to (re)initiate alkyl radical formation. The combined catalytic and organometallic studies evidenced a radical chain mechanism for alkyl–alkyl cross-coupling, which engages productive alkyl radical capture at stable (TMEDA)cobalt(II)–monoalkyl bromide and subsequent bond-forming reductive elimination. The competent (TMEDA)cobalt(II) dibromide precatalyst enabled alkyl–alkyl Negishi cross-coupling reactions of a variety of substrates, including tertiary 1-adamantyl bromides and secondary dialkylzinc reagents, demonstrating that the open-shell character of high-spin cobalt(II)–alkyl catalysts promotes successful, cross-selective alkyl–alkyl radical coupling.

item.title: Predicting CO 2 Reduction Selectivity on Large-Scale Cu–Pd Nanoparticles via a Multi-Scale Machine Learning Framework
item.description:
Abstract
The conventional computational approach to electrocatalyst evaluation has long been limited by its reliance on simplified slab models and adsorption energies on bare surfaces, which fail to capture the structural complexity of realistic nanoparticles (NPs) and the presence of adsorbates that decorates electrode surfaces under working conditions. To bridge this gap, we present a multi-scale computational framework that combines machine learning potential (MLP)-driven molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with the explicit realization of potential-dependent surface coverage and high-throughput evaluation of active sites. Applying this framework to the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) on Cu–Pd alloys, we generated realistic 8 nm NP morphologies using a SevenNet MLP trained from scratch and determined the coverage states and binding energies of key intermediates (CO*, H*, and OH*) across all surface sites using a zero-shot universal MLP. Our coverage-resolved evaluation reveals a systematic transformation of product selectivity across the composition–potential space, from formate production on Cu-rich NPs to CO evolution and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) on their Pd-rich counterparts. Notably, a discernible C1+ fraction emerges on the Cu3Pd alloy at intermediate overpotentials, reflecting the promotional effect of dilute Pd incorporation. This work establishes a methodology that bridges the gap between atomistic predictions and the structural and electrochemical complexity of working nanocatalysts, paving the way for more accurate in-silico discovery of electrocatalysts.

item.title: Bioinspired Multi-metallic Relay Catalyst for Efficient Nitrate Reduction and Zn-NO 3 – Battery Performance
item.description:
Abstract
Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (e-NO3– RR) to ammonia offers an effective pathway for environmental remediation and clean energy production. However, its efficiency is often constrained by sluggish multi-electron/proton transfer and mismatched intermediate adsorption. Herein, we report a bioinspired multi-metallic cobalt copper molybdate (CCM) catalyst that overcomes these limitations through a relay-type catalytic mechanism enabled by spatially distinct metal centers. In this architecture, Cu, Co, and Mo sites cooperatively orchestrate intermediate stabilization and proton activation in successive reaction steps, thereby facilitating an efficient cascade conversion of nitrate to ammonia. As a result, the optimized CCM catalyst achieves an ammonia yield rate of 2.6 mmol h–1 cm–2 and a Faradaic efficiency up to 92%. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses identify the synergistic interplay among the multiple metal active centers as the mechanistic basis for the enhanced nitrate-to-ammonia performance. Beyond half-cell evaluation, integration of the CCM catalyst into a Zn-NO3– battery delivers an output voltage of 1.34 V and a power density of 4.1 mW cm–2, demonstrating its viability for coupled ammonia synthesis and energy generation. This study identifies multi-metallic relay catalysis as an effective strategy for efficient electrocatalytic nitrate-to-ammonia conversion.

item.title: Temporally Distinguishing Photocatalytic Dynamics
item.description:
Abstract
Light can induce both photothermal and nonthermal catalytic activity in plasmonic nanoparticles, but the extent, timescale, and efficacy of these two mechanisms remain unresolved. Here, we introduce pump–pump photocatalysis, an adaptation of ultrafast excitation correlation spectroscopy in which incident laser pulses are split into two spatially and energetically equivalent pulses separated by a variable time delay. For a given reaction and catalyst, time-sensitive nonlinear enhancements in photocatalytic activity may be distinguished from time-insensitive responses as a function of time delay, pulse power, excitation wavelength, applied temperature, reactant pressure, and pulse asymmetry. In this way, the timescales of photothermal and nonthermal activity of any photocatalyst may be monitored on sub-picosecond to nanosecond timescales, and the conditions for optimal chemical reactivity may be discovered. To illustrate this technique, we perform ultrafast measurements of the ammonia decomposition reaction using a Cu–Ru antenna-reactor photocatalyst. Photothermal contributions exhibit little sensitivity to pulse delay, while nonthermal contributions are most apparent at low excitation intensity, moderate temperatures, and sub-nanosecond timescales. Here, nonlinear, nonthermal mechanisms enhance H2 production by a factor of up to eleven compared to when pulses overlap. This technique may be used to provide insightful in operando diagnostics and control of any photocatalyst for any chemical reaction while revealing the optimal distribution of light to maximize photocatalytic activity.

item.title: Iron-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Phosphonylation of Aliphatic Carboxylic Acids with Succinimidyl Phosphites as Bifunctional Reagents
item.description:
Abstract
Aliphatic carboxylic acids are abundant, stable, and cost-effective, rendering them ideal substrates for site-specific C(sp3)–P bond formation via decarboxylative pathways. However, the direct catalytic decarboxylative phosphonylation of these acids remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report that the use of dialkyl succinimidyl phosphites as bifunctional reagents enables the iron-catalyzed decarboxylative phosphonylation of aliphatic carboxylic acids to proceed smoothly at room temperature under visible light irradiation. The transformation accommodates primary, secondary, and tertiary alkyl acids, delivering the corresponding alkylphosphonates in satisfactory yields with broad functional group tolerance. A reaction mechanism involving photoinduced ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) of ferric carboxylates, β-scission of phosphoranyl radical intermediates leading to N–O bond cleavage, and single-electron oxidation of ferrous ions by succinimidyl radicals, is proposed.

item.title: Conformationally Locked Yttrium Indanosalan Complexes for Fast Isoselective Ring-Opening Polymerization of β-Butyrolactone at Elevated Temperatures
item.description:
Abstract
We report rigid yttrium indanosalan complexes for the high-temperature ring-opening polymerization of β-butyrolactone. Some of the complexes (isolated or obtained in situ) developed were able to polymerize β-butyrolactone with high isoselectivity (Pm = 0.88) and very high activity (TOF up to 135,000 h–1) at a polymerization temperature of 100 °C, at which the polymer remains in solution, facilitating its further processing. Polymerization at 30–60 °C yielded the poly(3-hydroxybutyrate)s with Pm up to 0.94. The roles of active site configuration and non-covalent interactions were studied experimentally and by DFT, which reproduced the enantiomorphic-site control and showed that the monomer was oriented by C–H···π and C–H···O contacts, rather than by N–H···O hydrogen bonding.

item.title: Tailoring Surface Defects in SBA-15 Via Heteroatom Distortion for Enhanced CO 2 -to-Methanol Yield
item.description:
Abstract
The conversion of CO2 to methanol presents a viable energy solution that mitigates greenhouse gas emissions by utilizing CO2 to produce fuel. In this work, the inert mesoporous silica material SBA-15 was strategically fine-tuned to serve as an active support by incorporating Ti into its framework, followed by the impregnation of CuNiGa into it, which enhances electron transfer between the constituent metals. This modification results in the formation of a Cu1.5Ni1.5Ga ternary alloy phase, which activates CO2 and facilitates H2 spillover. High-field (28.2 T) solid-state NMR spectroscopy has been applied to resolve local bonding environments of Ti, Si and Ga sites. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses confirm the formation of the ternary phase. The crucial metal–support interaction (MSI) was observed due to the formation of TiO2 nanoparticles at higher Ti loadings. Pyridine-IR (Py-IR) analysis reveals a progressive increase in the Lewis acidity of Ti-modified SBA-15 with increasing Ti loading. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and in situ Raman spectroscopy were conducted to probe the dynamic behavior of oxygen vacancies. CO2-to-methanol activity reached a high space-time yield (STY) of 1.97 gMeOH/gCuNiGa h at 275 °C and 45 bar, and it was attributed to MSI and the increased Lewis acidity. The interaction of reactant molecules with the catalysts were investigated using temperature-programmed desorption/reduction (TPD/TPR), and the mechanistic studies were performed using in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS).

item.title: Reverse Water Gas Shift Reaction over a Homogeneous Iron Catalyst and the Underlying Mechanism
item.description:
Abstract
The CO production by the reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction is a promising bridge between CO2 conversion and well-established C1 chemistry. Currently, heterogeneous catalysts are mostly reported for this reaction, which usually require high operating temperatures (above 600 °C) and encounter poor selectivity of CO at lower temperatures (below 400 °C). Homogeneous catalysis may offer distinct advantages at a low temperature. Nevertheless, only some noble metal homogeneous catalysts for this reaction have been reported to date. Herein, we report the iron phthalocyanine (FePc) as a homogeneous catalyst to selectively produce CO via the RWGS reaction in the N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) solvent. The reaction started at a low temperature of 120 °C with a CO selectivity of 98.1%, and high CO selectivity was attained under various conditions. Large-scale DFT calculations and control experiments revealed a tri-active-center mechanism, wherein the Fe center and Pc ligand separately and simultaneously activate CO2 and H2 and then cooperatively catalyze their conversion to CO and H2O. In addition, this work quantitatively demonstrates that the dispersion interactions between the catalyst and solvent molecules play a critical role in homogeneous transition-metal-catalyzed CO2 conversion reactions.

item.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Accelerates Rational Design of Dual-Site Catalysts for Synergistic Catalytic Aerobic Oxidative Synthesis of Benzimidazole
item.description:
Abstract
The aerobic oxidative synthesis of benzimidazole requires heterogeneous catalysts that combine high activity with practical stability. Because conventional catalyst optimization depends heavily on laborious experimental screening, we established an interpretable machine learning (ML) workflow to accelerate catalyst selection and identify the variables governing performance. An XGBoost model was trained to relate catalyst descriptors and reaction conditions to benzimidazole synthesis, and partial-dependence-plot (PDP) analysis was used to determine favorable catalyst compositions and operating windows. Guided by the model, we prepared the cobalt-based dual-site catalyst CoNP-CoSA@NC-800. Under mild conditions (90 °C, 9 h) with atmospheric air as the oxidant, this material delivered 100% conversion and 96% benzimidazole selectivity. It also tolerated a broad range of substrates and retained its activity during recycling. Control experiments and theoretical calculations indicate that the Co nanoparticle (CoNP) and Co single atom (CoSA) sites act cooperatively: the CoNP component modifies the d-band center and electronic structure of CoNP-CoSA@NC-800, thereby enhancing O2 adsorption and activation to facilitate benzimidazole formation.

item.title: Vacancy-Directed Phytate Coordination Couples Ni-Site Polarization with Interfacial Hydration for Durable Photoelectrochemical Seawater Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Photoelectrochemical seawater oxidation is limited by a coupled interfacial challenge: low-coordinated metal sites that favor hole utilization and oxygen evolution are also susceptible to chloride attack, whereas protective surface modification can compromise water access. Here, oxygen vacancies in amorphous NiCr2O4–x on α-Fe2O3 are repurposed to direct multidentate phytate coordination, constructing a molecular interface that couples Ni-site polarization with interfacial hydration. Catalyst-facing M–O–P coordination withdraws electron density from vacancy-activated Ni sites, strengthens interfacial polarization, accelerates hole delivery, and reconstructs oxygenated-intermediate bonding, lowering the free-energy requirement of the *O → *OOH step from 0.66 to 0.45 eV. Meanwhile, electrolyte-facing phosphate groups remain exposed as persistent hydrogen-bonding nodes, preferentially stabilize O-down interfacial water, and organize a continuous hydration network that preserves H2O/OH– accessibility while suppressing Cl– approach and adsorption. Operando infrared spectroscopy, in situ ATR-SEIRAS, molecular dynamics simulations, ion mapping, and dissolution analyses collectively connect this coupled solid–liquid interfacial regulation with accelerated intermediate turnover and reduced corrosion. The resulting photoanode delivers 4.43 mA cm–2 at 1.23 V versus RHE, operates for 300 h with negligible decay in alkaline simulated seawater, and retains 82% of its initial photocurrent after 200 h in alkaline real seawater. These results establish vacancy-directed molecular coordination as a strategy for coupling active-site polarization with hydration-mediated protection in durable seawater photooxidation.

item.title: Brønsted Acid Site-Mediated Proton Injection and Redistribution Regulate Phosphoric Acid Electrochemical Interfaces
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular control of the proton environment in phosphoric acid (PA) based electrochemical interfaces is critical for efficient proton transport and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), yet effective strategies for actively regulating this environment remain limited. Here, we show that Brønsted acid sites (BASs) in HY zeolite function as solid-state proton regulating centers that directly participate in and reorganize the interfacial PA hydrogen bond network. By combining ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations, free energy calculations, variable-temperature diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (VT-DRIFTS), and electrochemical measurements, we reveal a BAS-mediated proton injection and redistribution mechanism. The framework BAS proton transfers to an adjacent PA molecule, generating an excess proton defect that dynamically redistributes among neighboring PA molecules through hydrogen-bond-assisted proton hopping. The potential of mean force (PMF) along δ01 reveals a favorable free energy change for BAS to PA1 proton transfer (–0.122 eV), while density functional theory (DFT) calculations show lower electronic energies for representative PA-associated configurations, with PA2 exhibiting the lowest energy. AIMD simulations further demonstrate preferential excess-proton accommodation and dynamic redistribution within the PA network. VT-DRIFTS measurements reveal PA-induced changes in the temperature-dependent hydroxyl response of HY, while calculated harmonic infrared spectra of representative proton configurations provide molecular-level insight into interfacial proton interactions and hydrogen bond reorganization. Electrochemical measurements further show that HY incorporation reduces proton transport and ORR charge transfer resistances while increasing Pt electrochemical accessibility. These findings identify BAS-mediated proton injection and redistribution as a promising molecular strategy for regulating PA-based electrochemical interfaces.

item.title: Radical-Based Catalytic Transformations of 1-Azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes: Opportunities and Future Directions
item.description:
Abstract
1-Azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (ABBs) have emerged as versatile strained precursors to saturated, three-dimensional azetidine scaffolds that are increasingly valuable in modern drug discovery. This Perspective contends that the recent proliferation of radical-based catalytic platforms, encompassing photoredox, metallaphotoredox, energy-transfer, and electrochemical manifolds, serves as an effective complement to classical polar chemistry, enabling diverse transformations and the construction of sterically congested carbon–carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds through distinct reactivity profiles. We illustrate how open-shell intermediates enable the precise, regiodivergent, and multicomponent construction of sterically congested azetidines and azabicyclo[n.1.1]alkanes. We argue that while several mechanistic patterns have now been proposed, their underlying reactivity principles remain incompletely understood, and the broader synthetic potential remains largely underexplored. We therefore chart a forward-looking agenda: the development of alternative radical transformations, the expansion of radical coupling partners to include abundant and readily available feedstocks, the integration of electrochemistry for scalable and catalyst-free processes, and the design of radical relay sequences that access architecturally complex bridged azabicycles beyond simple azetidines. By framing these frontiers as both timely and achievable, we aim to catalyze the evolution of radical ABB chemistry from a specialized tool into a broadly enabling strategy for constructing the nitrogen-containing, sp3-rich chemical space that next-generation drug discovery demands.

item.title: Light-Driven Reconstruction of MoS 2 Nanosheets Boosts Photothermal Reverse Water Gas Shift Reaction with Near-Unity Selectivity
item.description:
Abstract
In-depth understanding of the reconstruction behaviors during photothermal reactions is of paramount importance for the design of highly efficient photothermal catalysts. Here, we demonstrate the photothermal effect-induced reconstruction of MoS2 nanosheets during the photothermal reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction. Specifically, under the operating photothermal reaction conditions, the MoS2 nanosheet catalyst undergoes rapid surface temperature increase up to around 380 °C, which can react with the H2 gas to produce in-plane S vacancies, thereby leading to the reconstruction of MoS2 nanosheets for enhanced RWGS reaction activity. An approximately 7.8 mmol g–1 h–1 evolution rate with a near-unity selectivity of CO (>99%) is achieved over MoS2 nanosheets during 100 h stability testing under flow-bed reaction and atmospheric pressure. Detailed structural characterizations combined with density functional theory simulations unravel that the photothermal effect-induced reconstruction of MoS2 can facilitate the charge separation and adsorption of reactants, lower the energy barrier of the *COOH intermediate, and meanwhile, improve the H2 dissociation ability for promoting the RWGS reaction.

item.title: Nonlinear Field-Reorganization Coupling Dictates Cation-Steered Proton Transfer at Electrified Interfaces
item.description:
Abstract
Electrolyte cations in the electric double layer strongly influence electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to multicarbon products, yet the microscopic origin of this cation effect remains elusive. Using metadynamics-biased ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, we identify a cation-driven electrostatic traction mechanism, where the cation-induced local electric field promotes the interfacial water activation and directly steers nascent protons toward adsorbed *CO2 via an Eley–Rideal path, effectively bypassing the Volmer H adsorption intermediate as the dominant channel under these interfacial conditions. At the electrified interface, strong electronic coupling in this inner-sphere proton-coupled electron transfer process renormalizes the classical solvent reorganization energy to effective quantum reorganization energy, flattening the reaction potential energy surface. We further establish an adiabatic Marcus–Stark framework by nonlinearly coupling the interfacial electric field with the effective reorganization energy, which quantitatively accounts for a substantial part of the experimentally observed exponential acceleration of C2 product formation with K+ over Li+ and identifies interfacial proton supply as an important rate-modulating factor within the broader C2 reaction network. This finding partially decouples reaction kinetics from intermediate binding energy scaling relations, providing a physical framework for manipulating electrochemical selectivity through interfacial microenvironment engineering.

item.title: Modular Synthesis of α-Tertiary Amines Enabled by Nickel-Catalyzed Reductive Alkylation of N -unprotected Ketimines
item.description:
Abstract
The straightforward construction of sterically hindered α-tertiary primary amines remains a stubborn challenge in organic synthesis. Although a wide array of approaches for the synthesis of this motif has been developed, the leveraging of ketimines as an amine source is underexplored. General reductive alkylative additions of unactivated alkyl halides to N-unprotected ketimines remain unknown. Herein, we disclose a nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling between N-unprotected heteroaryl ketimines and readily available alkyl halides, including primary, secondary, and tertiary ones, to directly furnish diverse primary amines with steric congestion without attendant deprotection sequences. This synthetic protocol circumvents the use of preformed organometallic reagents, leading to broad functional group tolerance and high step-economy. Preliminary mechanistic investigations support a radical-type cross-coupling pathway of N-H ketimines with unactivated alkyl radicals involving a Ni(I)/Ni(II)/Ni(III) redox cycle. The practicality of this method has been demonstrated in successful application in the synthesis of various cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors.

item.title: Cyclative Carbon Quaternization of Alkyl Boronic Esters via Copper-Catalyzed Aminyl Radical Transfer
item.description:
Abstract
Despite the rich chemistry of alkyl boronic esters (alkyl Bpins) in C–B bond transformations, carbon quaternization via concurrent C–B and C–H bond scission on the boron-substituted carbon has remained elusive. Herein, we report a copper-catalyzed aminyl radical-mediated cyclative C-quaternization of alkyl Bpins with acrylamides to access valuable carbo- and spirocyclic scaffolds. Central to this transformation is a sequential C–B/C–H bond-cleavage, in which ART triggers C–B cleavage and HAT enables site-selective C–H functionalization. The method has a broad substrate scope, high functional group tolerance, and exquisite site selectivity and allows late-stage diversification of drugs and natural products. Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations were conducted to elucidate the underlying reaction mechanism. These studies support the generation of aminyl radicals via Cu–N bond homolysis, which is effective for ART, and rationalize selective 1,5-HAT and copper-mediated PCET in the key cyclization step.

item.title: Palladium(II)-Catalyzed Denitrogenation of Alkyl Diazirines
item.description:
Abstract
[PdCl2(NCPh)2] catalyzes the denitrogenation of mono(alkyl) diazirines in CDCl3 at 25 °C for 16 h to form the corresponding alkene in up to 70% yield. Reaction of (4-fluorophenyl)diazirine with a catalytic amount of [PdCl2(NCPh)2] (20 mol %) and excess styrene forms 1-(4-fluorophenyl)-2-phenylcyclopropane in 48% yield (cis/trans = 6.7:1). Kinetic experiments, in situ analysis of palladium coordination complexes, and DFT calculations support a mechanism for Pd(II)-catalyzed denitrogenation of benzyl diazirine involving C─N oxidative addition (ΔG‡ = 22.4 kcal/mol) of a four-coordinate trans-palladium σ-diazirine complex to form a five-coordinate Pd(IV) diazometallacyclobutane complex. Subsequent Pd─C bond cleavage (ΔG‡ = 8.8 kcal/mol) to form an N-bound diazo complex followed by isomerization to the corresponding C-bound diazo complex, presumably via intermolecular ligand exchange, and facile (ΔG‡ = 4.2 kcal/mol) extrusion of dinitrogen forms a trans-palladium alkylidene complex. Concerted, 1,2-H migration (ΔG‡ = 5.0 kcal/mol) forms the corresponding four-coordinate palladium π-styrene complex.

item.title: Elucidation of Pathways in the Conversion of CO 2 -Rich Syngas to Methanol over Cu-Based Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
The efficient conversion of CO2-rich syngas to fuels remains challenging because of distinct thermodynamics between CO2 and CO hydrogenation. In this work, we investigate the structure–performance relationship and reaction mechanism of CO2-rich syngas conversion to methanol over a series of Cu-based catalysts, with CO2 contents ranging from 4% to 25%. We find that the CuZnZr catalyst exhibits the best overall performance because of the enhanced adsorption/activation of CO and CO2, resulting from the strengthened Cu–oxide interaction and promoted Cu–ZnO–ZrOx interface. The catalytic performance of CuZnZr is highly sensitive to both the Zn/Zr ratio and the CO2 content in the feed gas, with a Cu/Zn/Zr ratio of 6:3:1, giving the highest activity. We find that CO is mainly adsorbed on Cu sites, whereas CO2 is preferentially activated at Cu–ZnO/ZrOx interfacial sites to form formate and methoxy species. In CO2-containing syngas, CO*, HCOO*, and CH3O* coexist on the surface, and a small amount of CO2 effectively promotes the hydrogenation of HCOO* to CH3O*. Isotope-labeled experiments further confirm that CO2 not only undergoes the reverse water–gas shift reaction to form CO but also directly participates in methanol formation through oxygen-containing intermediates. Both the carbon and oxygen atoms in methanol can originate from the CO2 in feed gas, demonstrating a coupled hydrogenation mechanism involving both CO and CO2. In addition, a trace amount of water vapor increases the surface coverage of both HCOO* and CH3O* and promotes methanol formation, rather than only acting as a spectator. Therefore, the improved catalytic performance of CuZnZr originates from the optimized Cu–ZnO–ZrOx interface and the cooperative transformation of CO*, HCOO*, and CH3O*. These findings provide mechanistic insights and guidance for the design of efficient Cu-based catalysts in the direct methanol synthesis from CO2-rich syngas.

item.title: Adaptive Dynamic Evolution of Substitutional Pt Single Atoms in CeO 2 for CO Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Platinum-substitutional ceria solid solutions (PtxCe1–xO2) have attracted considerable attention owing to their high stability and activity for low-temperature CO oxidation. However, their catalytic behavior and reactant-induced structural evolution under reaction conditions remain under debate. Here, we investigate the CO-induced structural evolution of substitutional Pt single-atom sites in CeO2(111) and their dynamically catalytic activity for low-temperature CO oxidation by means of density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Our results show that the commonly proposed octahedrally coordinated Pt species are unstable in a CO atmosphere since CO adsorbed on Pt readily reacts with lattice oxygen with a low energy barrier. The resulting CO2 formation induces a dynamic evolution of the Pt coordination environment, driving the transformation from octahedral coordination to a more energetically stable square-planar configuration. In addition, oxygen vacancies (VO) and CO adsorption synergistically promote the displacement of substitutional Pt atoms, leading to the formation of distorted Pt–CO complexes adjacent to vacancy sites that serve as the active centers for CO oxidation. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) and deep-potential molecular dynamics (DPMD) simulations further verify that the octahedral-to-square-planar dynamic evolution occurs spontaneously, while similar coordination evolution on the various ceria facets indicates that this behavior is not limited to CeO2(111) but is a general feature of Pt1-substituted CeO2. Further experimental characterization results corroborate the calculated coordination evolution of Pt sites and support the proposed dynamic structural transformation. These findings provide atomistic insights into the reaction-induced structural evolution of Pt species in CeO2 and clarify the origin of the catalytic activity of Pt-substituted ceria for low-temperature CO oxidation.

item.title: From Sensor to Catalyst: Heme-Dependent Oxidative N -Demethylase Redefines Per-ARNT-Sim-Domain Chemistry via Amine Oxidase Mechanisms for Dimethylamine Demethylation, Vital N–C Bond Cleavage in Global N -Cycle
item.description:
Abstract
Microbial N–C bond cleavage plays a vital role in the nitrogen biogeochemical cycle. Heme-dependent oxidative N-demethylase (HODM), an enzyme identified within the Per-ARNT-Sim (PAS) domain family, challenges the traditional view of PAS domains as merely sensory modules by catalyzing the dimethylamine (DMA) demethylation to methylamine (MA) and formaldehyde via N–C bond dissociation. In this study, we employed density functional calculations to investigate the mechanistic landscape of the HODM reaction across multiple spin states. Among nine mechanistic pathways examined, two (mechanisms A1 and A3) proceeding on the doublet-state surface were found to be viable, mainly involving (1) addition of an electron to the enzyme-substrate complex generating Fe(III)–O22– anion, (2) proton transfer from Arg224 forming Fe(III)––OOH (Cpd 0), (3) homolytic O─O bond cleavage producing heme high-valent O═Fe(IV)(Por) (Cpd II) and •OH radical, (4) hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) from DMA to •OH yielding water, and (5) second HAT from DMA to Cpd II producing imine that hydrolyzes nonenzymatically to MA and formaldehyde. The DMA hydrogen abstraction by •OH is rate-limiting. Our findings establish HODM as an amine oxidase with •OH as the initial active species to abstract substrate hydrogens, instead of a monooxygenase using high-valent iron(IV)–oxo. Cpd 0 could not work as the H-abstraction species. Without an electron gained, the Fe(III)–O2•– superoxide radical is unable to initiate the HODM reaction. The revelation of HODM nature expands the PAS chemistry and enriches the understanding of enzymatic N–C bond dissociation and heme chemistry.

item.title: Halogen Fluorine Unlocks Ru Activity for Olefins Production from Syngas
item.description:
Abstract
Olefins production from syngas via Fischer–Tropsch synthesis requires catalysts that favor olefins formation, maintain intrinsic activity, and suppress CO2 and CH4 formation. Sodium-promoted ruthenium nanoparticles shift the product distribution toward α-olefins but suppress Ru activity by more than 90%, necessitating higher Ru loadings. We show that incorporating inorganic fluorine into Na-promoted Ru catalysts increases activity 2.5-fold while maintaining 72.1% α-olefins selectivity and ∼5.0% combined selectivity to CO2 and CH4. At a Ru loading of 1.26 wt %, the catalyst achieves a Ru time yield of 1.14 molCO·gRu–1·h–1 and olefins space-time yield of 1516.1 g·molRu–1·h–1, outperforming most reported Ru-based catalysts. Fluorine also restores activity in Fe- and Co-based systems. Mechanistic studies indicate that surface Na–F cation–anion pairs modulate the electronic structure, weaken Ru-CO binding, and generate hydrogen species that accelerate CO activation and suppress olefins hydrogenation. This work established a halogen-mediated strategy to address the activity–selectivity trade-off in sodium-promoted syngas conversion.

item.title: Non-Thermal Plasma-Assisted CH 4 –CO 2 Co-Conversion: A Reservoir of Surface Species is the Key to Selective Liquid Product Formation
item.description:
Abstract
Non-thermal plasma (NTP) catalysis enables the direct co-conversion of CH4 and CO2 into thermodynamically limited liquid products under mild conditions. However, achieving high selectivity toward liquid products and clarifying the role of the catalyst in steering product distribution remain significant challenges. Here we uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism governing selectivity in plasma catalysis: the formation of a reservoir of strongly adsorbed surface species that evolves during reaction and dynamically controls liquid-product formation. We investigated the catalytic performance, catalyst structure, plasma properties, and surface species during time-dependent liquid methanol production—in addition to valuable syngas and C2 hydrocarbons in the gas stream—over an α-Fe2O3 catalyst. Stable catalyst structure and plasma conditions were unable to explain the transient product selectivity towards methanol. Instead, in situ plasma–IR studies revealed that strongly bound C═O and C–H species progressively accumulated with time-on-stream (TOS) and correlated with the observed increase in methanol yield. The strongly bound C═O and C–H species are proposed to enhance methanol selectivity by modifying the surface Brønsted and Lewis acidity, promoting methoxy hydrogenation, and weakening methanol adsorption. Studying the plasma interaction of select reaction species (CH4, CO2, CO, methanol, acetaldehyde, and acetic acid) with the catalyst surface showed that the main liquid product, methanol, was responsible for populating the surface with hydrogenated carbonyl species that boosted its own production. A methanol-plasma pretreatment was envisioned and implemented to preload a reservoir of the C═O and C–H species on the surface of α-Fe2O3, resulting in a significant improvement in catalyst performance for selective methanol production. After 8 h TOS, the treated catalyst exhibited a 30% relative increase in selectivity and a threefold increase in methanol yield compared to the untreated catalyst, offering a promising route toward highly selective liquid product formation. Additionally, the methanol–plasma pretreatment to boost methanol production was extended to other metal oxide catalysts, highlighting the broad versatility and potential of this strategy across a wide range of plasma catalyst systems.

item.title: Durability Assessment of α-MnO 2 Nanorods for Alkaline ORR under Application-Relevant Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
This study investigates the durability of α-MnO2, one of the most cost-effective catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in alkaline media. A comprehensive set of various characterization techniques, including identical location transmission electron microscopy (IL-TEM), differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS), rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE), and online inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) coupled to both flow cell and gas diffusion electrode (GDE) half-cell, was employed. In addition, accelerated stress test (AST) measurements in the GDE half-cell followed by post mortem X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and TEM analysis were performed. Three electrolyte and temperature combinations ranging from standard lab conditions to application-relevant conditions were systematically investigated. The results reveal that Mn dissolution occurs under oxygen-free conditions due to oxidation-state transitions of the catalyst, whereas under oxygen, it is further accelerated by degradation processes associated with peroxide formation as a byproduct of the ORR, particularly at higher ORR overpotentials. Both increasing KOH concentration and temperature significantly enhance Mn dissolution due to accelerated Mn reduction and dissolution kinetics. Despite the increased dissolution, the condition of 4.0 M KOH at 25 °C exhibits the highest ORR activity after 5000 AST cycles. This apparent discrepancy is attributed to surface roughening of the catalyst, leading to an increased electrochemically active surface area. Overall, the results demonstrate that α-MnO2 exhibits promising initial ORR activity but undergoes substantial Mn dissolution under operating conditions. These findings provide mitigation strategies to limit catalyst degradation and improve operational durability.

item.title: A Fungal Hyaluronate Lyase with a Distinct Catalytic Machinery Expands the Polysaccharide Lyase Landscape
item.description:
Abstract
Hyaluronic acid (HA) is a major glycosaminoglycan of the vertebrate extracellular matrix whose biological functions depend strongly on its molecular weight. Controlled depolymerization of HA into defined oligosaccharides is therefore of considerable biomedical and biotechnological interest. Although bacterial HA lyases have been extensively characterized, fungal HA-degrading enzymes remain poorly understood, and none has been structurally assigned to a defined CAZy family. Here, we identify and characterize PlLya44, an HA lyase secreted by the filamentous fungus Purpureocillium lilacinum. The enzyme was detected in the fungal secretome, produced in Pichia pastoris, and shown to efficiently depolymerize high molecular weight HA, generating mainly unsaturated oligosaccharides with both even- and odd-numbered products. Product analysis supports a predominantly processive endolytic mode of action distinct from the classical exo-processive mechanism of bacterial HA lyases. The crystal structure of PlLya44 uncovers an α-helical α6/α6 barrel fold characteristic of the (α/α)n toroid superfamily, harboring an elongated polarity-partitioned catalytic cleft. Structural comparisons and sequence similarity network analyses demonstrate that PlLya44 does not cluster with any currently defined polysaccharide lyase (PL) family, supporting its classification as the founding member of a distinct PL family. Ligand-bound structures, mutagenesis, ensemble refinement, and molecular dynamics reveal a reorganized catalytic architecture, reversing substrate orientation relative to previously characterized HA lyases. Together, these findings provide structural insight into a fungal HA lyase, uncover a previously unrecognized catalytic strategy for HA depolymerization, and establish PlLya44 as the founding member of a hitherto undescribed PL family, expanding the enzymatic landscape of glycosaminoglycan-active enzymes.

item.title: Interactive Learning with Low‑Performance Data for Accurate CO 2 Reduction Catalyst Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Emerging machine learning (ML) approaches offer transformative strategies to accelerate discovery for challenging objectives, such as developing practical catalysts through rational design. We propose an iterative learning framework and strategy that effectively enhances the predictive capability of the ML model, thereby accelerating catalyst development. By leveraging low-performance catalytic results, we have proven a practical, scalable framework for data-efficient catalyst development and for the broader application of ML methods in heterogeneous catalysis. The ML approach effectively captures the intrinsic relationship between metal type/content and catalytic performance, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy through iterative optimization. The case example regards the development of metal-supported catalysts for CO2 reduction. The results show that incorporating low-performance catalytic results into the iterative learning process markedly improves the predictive accuracy of the random forest (RF) model (R2 increased from 0.80 to 0.86, and mean square error (RMSE) decreased from 1.20% to 0.89%). The deviations between the experimental and predicted values for the CO2 reduction performance of the four catalysts identified through this approach were all less than 2%, demonstrating the model's reliability and predictive capability. Among them, the 1.5Pt2Fe/TiO2-R catalyst exhibited high CO2 reduction activity and long-term stability (>200 h), highlighting the practical potential of ML-guided catalyst design. The use of low-performance catalytic data outperforms high-performance ones in improving predictive accuracy when coupled with a suitable iterative learning framework, providing mechanistic insight into how they help the model define the boundaries of the feasible performance region.

item.title: MoO x as an Oxidized Incorporation Modulates Nickel Sites for Efficient H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis at 200 mA cm –2
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis via the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e– ORR) enables on-site production, yet its practical application is hindered by the scarcity of catalysts that can simultaneously deliver high selectivity, activity, and stability at industrial current densities. Here, we report molybdenum incorporation into nickel oxide, where Mo is predominantly present as atomically dispersed, oxygen-coordinated Mo species (denoted as MoOx). The resulting MoOx–NiO catalyst features a hybrid crystalline–amorphous structure. Spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal that MoOx induces a localized electron redistribution, generating electron-rich Ni sites with a formal valence below + 2 (Ni2–x) adjacent to MoOx as key active sites. These Ni2–x sites tune the adsorption free energy of the critical OOH intermediate and favor the 2e– pathway over the competing 4e– pathway. The MoOx–NiO achieves >95% H2O2 selectivity over a potential range of 0.25–0.70 V vs RHE and a high production rate of 34.8 ± 0.8 mol gcat–1 h–1 at an industrial current density of 200 mA cm–2 in a flow cell, together with high Faradic efficiency and long-term operational stability. These findings show that engineering the chemical state and oxygen coordination of a dopant can modulate the local electronic structures of host metal sites and thereby influence catalytic pathways, providing a strategy for the design of advanced oxide electrocatalysts.

item.title: Oxygen Vacancy Distribution as a Structural Switch for Oxygen Cycling: A Local Oxygen Chemical Potential Descriptor for Methane Oxidative Coupling on SrTiO 3
item.description:
Abstract
Oxygen species evolution is central to the catalytic performance of oxidative coupling of methane (OCM), yet understanding and controlling this evolution remains a major challenge. SrTiO3 is a promising OCM catalyst due to its high C2 selectivity and stability but suffers from low activity. Here, DFT calculations combined with kMC simulations were employed to investigate facet-dependent oxygen species cycling on SrTiO3. Our findings reveal that SrTiO3(100)-Ti is the most favorable facet, sustaining a regenerable oxygen cycle (“O2− → OV → O22− → Ti-OH → O2−”). The local oxygen chemical potential (μO) is further identified as a thermodynamic descriptor linking oxygen stability with CH4* activation ability, following the order OV > O22− > Ti-OH > O2−. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of OV acts as a structural switch, directing two competing Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) cycles. kMC simulations reveal that the peroxide-mediated pathway dominates under operando conditions, whereas the overall activity is limited by the low activity of O2− and the accumulation of inert OlatH that further poisons active sites. Notably, B-site La doping effectively overcomes this bottleneck by activating OlatH and increasing the μO of O2− from –9.12 eV to –6.57 eV, which enhances the CH4(g) turnover frequency from 4.79 × 10−1 to 2.40 s−1 at 1073.15 K. These results establish μO and oxygen vacancy distribution as general design principles for perovskite oxide catalysts, offering a promising strategy to enhance OCM activity.

item.title: Rh δ+ Anchored on Rh–Fe Bimetallic Nano-islands Ensures Highly Efficient CO Hydrogenation to Ethanol
item.description:
Abstract
The direct synthesis of ethanol from syngas faces a key challenge: achieving high selectivity at high CO conversion while elucidating the catalytic reaction mechanism. Here, we develop a catalyst comprising highly dispersed Rh–Fe bimetallic nano-islands supported on mixed-phase TiO2, which overcomes the trade-off between catalytic activity and ethanol selectivity, achieving an ethanol selectivity of 62.5% among all carbon-containing products at a CO conversion of 55.8%. Meanwhile, CO2 selectivity is greatly reduced to 8.1%. Mechanistic studies reveal that the breakthrough stems from the enhanced density of interfacial active sites, that the Fe species modulate the local electronic environment to optimize the Rhδ+/Rh0 ratio, and Rhδ+ species in contact with the TiO2 support are stably anchored via the formation of FeOx–Rhδ+–Ov–Ti3+ interfacial sites. The in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS), chemical transient kinetics (CTK), and density functional theory (DFT) characterizations reveal that the surface Rh0 sites facilitate CO dissociation and hydrogenation, whereas the FeOx–Rhδ+–Ov–Ti3+ interfacial sites promote the coupling of CHx with CHxO while suppressing the CO* + O → CO2 pathway. This work provides a route for suppressing CO2 formation and enhancing ethanol production in syngas conversion.

item.title: Relating Cu Phase Transitions to Selectivity Recovery During Pulsed CO 2 Reduction on Gas Diffusion Electrodes
item.description:
Abstract
Pulsed electrochemical CO2 reduction on Cu catalysts represents a promising strategy to mitigate catalyst degradation and sustain high selectivity toward multicarbon (C2+) products. However, developing a detailed mechanistic understanding of the oxidative pulses remains challenging due to the inability to resolve the Cu oxidation state and the local electrolyte pH in the vicinity of the catalyst, especially inside a porous gas diffusion electrode. In this study, we investigate the impact of different potential pulse profiles on the recovery of CO and C2+ product selectivity, the latter representing C–C coupling. The potential-pH trajectories of the pulses are mapped onto calculated potential-pH Cu phase diagrams for CO2-saturated aqueous KCl and KHCO3 electrolytes to identify the thermodynamically accessible Cu phases during pulses. We show that abrupt pulses at a local alkaline pH lead to simultaneous C2+ and CO recovery. In contrast, quasi-adiabatic pulses, where the local pH remains equilibrated with the bulk pH, recover CO selectivity independently of C2+ products. Furthermore, in acidic KCl electrolytes, where no Cu oxide is thermodynamically accessible during a quasi-adiabatic pulse, the recovery of C2+ is attributed to Cu dissolution and redeposition. Importantly, this finding demonstrates that the formation of a Cu oxide phase, even temporarily during the pulse, is not required for C–C coupling. In contrast, in KHCO3 electrolyte, the formation of a Cu oxide phase remains thermodynamically accessible during pulses. Moreover, we show that the oxidative charge of the pulse recovering CO selectivity scales with prior reduction time, hypothesized to be a removal of surface poisoning species. Our findings enable rational design of pulse protocols based on electrolyte-, potential-, and pH-resolved Cu phase diagrams and provide a framework that can be extended to other catalysts and electrolytes.

item.title: Charge Transfer Engineering in Covalent Organic Frameworks for Red Visible Light-Driven Coenzyme Interconversion
item.description:
Abstract
Precise photocatalytic modulation of the NAD+/NADH redox balance is critical for advancing both biocatalytic cascade reactions and photodynamic therapy, yet this goal remains elusive due to the scarcity of efficient, broad-spectrum photocatalysts with orthogonal redox regulation capabilities. Herein, we report a bifunctional covalent organic framework-polyoxometalate (COF-POM) composite that enables bidirectional photocatalytic interconversion between NAD+ and NADH under red visible light irradiation, achieving 77.0% yield for NADH regeneration and nearly quantitative conversion in NADH oxidation. Strikingly, cyt c-mediated anaerobic NADH oxidation was successfully realized, enabling spatiotemporally precise modulation of the intracellular NAD+/NADH redox balance. Mechanistic investigations reveal that POM integration synergistically reinforces the built-in electric field of the COF matrix, substantially accelerating photogenerated charge separation and interfacial transfer kinetics. This work establishes a generalizable strategy for constructing high-performance photocatalysts to enable precise NAD+/NADH redox balance regulation for future tumor metabolic intervention.

item.title: Beneficial Reduction of Surface Compositional Complexity in High-Entropy Oxide Oxygen Evolution Reaction Catalysts into a Ternary Phase
item.description:
Abstract
Cost-competitive green hydrogen production via water electrolysis is limited by the scalability and economics of electrolyzers, particularly regarding the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrocatalyst. High-entropy oxides hold significant promise, yet the drivers of activity and stability are debated due to challenges in characterizing the catalytically relevant surface. Addressing this, we present the comprehensive surface-specific quantification of chemical and coordination evolution in compositionally complex high-entropy Ni/Co/Fe/Mn/Cr (hydr)oxide electrocatalysts using synchrotron-based X-ray spectroscopies assisted by charge transfer multiplet calculations. An electrochemically driven surface transformation to ternary Ni/Co/Fe or Ni/Co/Mn (oxy)hydroxide in alkaline media is revealed to enable long-term efficient OER performance. This beneficial reduction in compositional complexity, and thus entropy, is induced by leaching of Cr, Mn, and Fe, enriching catalytically active octahedrally coordinated nickel and cobalt species, and is accelerated by a short-range-ordered phase (X-ray amorphous) compared to the crystalline counterpart. These findings highlight the importance of characterizing the surface chemical evolution of high-entropy materials and guide the engineering of next-generation compositionally complex transition-metal-based OER catalysts.

item.title: Graph-Guided C–C Coupling Pathways from Reaction Networks to Excited-State Dynamics in CO 2 -to-C 2 H 4 Photoelectroreduction
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient photoelectrocatalytic CO2 reduction to multi-carbon products remains challenging due to branched reaction networks, multiple proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps, and competing C–C coupling pathways. Here, we establish a multiscale framework integrating graph theory, physics-informed graph neural networks (CatalGNN), constant-potential ab initio molecular dynamics (cp-AIMD), nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD), and real-time time-dependent density functional theory (rt-TDDFT) to resolve CO2-to-C2H4 conversion on a Cu-anchored polymeric carbon nitride (Cu@PCN) catalyst. First, a heterogeneous directed bipartite graph reaction network systematically enumerates all complete pathways within the predefined reaction network. These pathways are encoded into CatalGNN, where potential-dependent edge features are updated via the computational hydrogen electrode relation using the pathway energetic span as the activity descriptor, allowing GNNExplainer to identify the performance-controlling elementary steps. The thermodynamic screening flags *CO-*CO dimerization as the most favorable coupling pathway. Crucially, cp-AIMD and NAMD simulations reveal that the pre-coupling CuN4@*CO-*CO precursor contains CO-derived 2π* antibonding states above the conduction-band minimum, serving as hot electron acceptors under photoexcitation. Hot-electron relaxation into these states occurs within 50 fs, providing a rapid electronic pre-activation channel. After C–C coupling, the *COCO intermediate introduces localized trap states that reshape carrier recombination dynamics. Notably, the spin-down channel exhibits a carrier lifetime of 16.4 ps, nearly three times longer than that of the spin-up channel, thereby sustaining localized charge at the reaction center for subsequent PCET steps. Finally, to bypass the thermodynamic bottleneck of *CO hydrogenation, rt-TDDFT simulations uncover a photoinduced radical mechanism where femtosecond laser excitation drives direct *CO hydrogenation and subsequent trapping of the *CHO radical at the CuN4 site through robust Cu–C bonding. This multiscale paradigm shows that efficient photoelectrocatalytic CO2-to-C2H4 conversion is governed by the synergy of pathway thermodynamics, potential-dependent electronic structures, spin-selective carrier lifetimes, and photoinduced radical chemistry, offering generalizable guidance for designing advanced multi-carbon products.

item.title: Asymmetric Convergent Assembly of Atropisomers Bearing Three Chiral Elements via Rhodium-Catalyzed Conjugate Addition
item.description:
Abstract
Atropisomers bearing multiple chiral elements offer diverse molecular architectures for the development of functional molecules; however, their catalytic asymmetric synthesis remains highly challenging. In this work, we report a catalytic asymmetric method for the efficient synthesis of atropisomers bearing three distinct chiral elements. This method employs a chiral rhodium catalyst to simultaneously control the stereodynamic axis of biarylhemiboronic esters, the remote desymmetrization of proatropisomeric maleimides, and the construction of a carbon stereocenter, affording chiral products containing a chiral C–C axis, a chiral C–N or N–N axis, and a carbon stereocenter in high yields with high stereoselectivities. Furthermore, we demonstrated the utility of the resulting scaffold through product derivatization and the development of an azophenol-based intramolecular charge-transfer probe.
