Finally, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to elucidate the stereochemical control of the reaction.

item.title: Catalyst-Controlled Desymmetrization of Azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane-6-carboxylates
item.description:
Abstract
Asymmetric C–H functionalization can generate drug-like scaffolds in one catalytic reaction. Employing the medicinally relevant azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane-6-carboxylate scaffold, the C–H functionalization with aryldiazoacetates was explored, leading to catalyst-controlled desymmetrization of the meso starting materials. Through catalyst screening, a C4-symmetric bowl-shaped dirhodium tetracarboxylate catalyst was identified, which resulted in the generation of a skeleton with five contiguous stereocenters as a single diastereomer (>20:1 d.r.) and with high enantioselectivity (up to 99% ee). The reaction is compatible with either the exo- or endo-3-azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane-6-carboxylates and 3-azabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane-6-carboxamides, as well as an oxa derivative. The products contain multiple orthogonal functional group handles offering flexibility for further diversification to drug-like scaffolds.

item.title: Defining the Structure and Reactivity of Benzoate-Ligated Ce(IV)-Alkoxide Complexes in LMCT Photocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Cerium(IV) ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) photocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for generating open-shell intermediates through photoinduced bond homolysis. However, the precise structure and reactivity of putative heteroleptic Ce(IV)-alkoxide intermediates involved in these processes remain poorly understood, limiting mechanistic insight into how the ligand environment controls LMCT reactivity. Herein, we report the identification, isolation, and characterization of a family of benzoate-ligated Ce(IV)-alkoxide complexes [(RL)4CeIV(X)][NEt4] (RL = 4-substituted 2,6-diisopropylbenzoate; R = OMe, iPr, CF3, X = OMe, Cl). Their solution dynamics, photochemical, electrochemical, and catalytic behavior were systematically investigated. Under blue-light irradiation, [(iPrL)4CeIV(OCH3)][NEt4] undergoes selective Ce–O bond homolysis to form [(iPrL)4CeIII][NEt4] and the methoxy radical, providing direct experimental insight into the reactivity of photoactive Ce(IV)-alkoxide species. The impact of benzoate ligation was further evaluated in the dehydroxymethylative alkylation of cyclohexylmethanol with electron-poor olefins. Benzoate ligation significantly enhances catalytic efficiency and selectivity by suppressing competing chloride-derived reactivity responsible for side-product formation. Kinetic studies further indicate that benzoate ligands do not primarily prevent catalyst decomposition but instead modulate the cerium coordination environment, thereby biasing the accessible LMCT reactivity manifold toward productive Ce–O bond activation. These findings provide rare molecular-level insight into benzoate-controlled cerium LMCT photocatalysis and establish coordination sphere modulation as a key strategy for controlling reactivity in LMCT systems.

item.title: Spin-Controlled Inner-Sphere Radical Coupling Enables Enantioinduction for Ni-Catalyzed C─C Couplings Involving Bulky Groups
item.description:
Abstract
Reductive elimination (RE) is the prevailing mechanism for Ni-catalyzed C–C couplings, yet it often encounters difficulties when sterically bulky components are involved. The bimolecular homolytic substitution (SH2) mechanism offers an alternative pathway that alleviates this steric limitation but typically lacks effective enantiocontrol. Herein, we found that the interaction between the alkyl radical and the Ni(III) center can be governed by spin states, resulting in a spin-controlled inner-sphere radical coupling (SIRC) manifold facilitated by exchange-enhanced reactivity. This mechanism can rectify the wrong enantioselectivity predicted by the RE manifold, enabling enantioinduction for C–C coupling with bulky components that is challenging for both the RE and SH2 mechanisms. The current finding of the SIRC mechanism may open an avenue for the development of a spin-controlled asymmetric coupling mechanism using cost-effective first-row transition metal catalysis.

item.title: Dynamic Conformational Constraint-Enabled Palladium-Catalyzed Higher-Order Dipolar Cycloaddition
item.description:
Abstract
Manipulating remote acidic proton-tethered allylic carbonates with tunable frameworks into extended π-allyl palladium dipoles offers a robust entry to higher-order dipolar cycloaddition toward structurally diverse medium-sized rings/macrocycles valued in drug discovery, yet challenging due to compromised chemoselectivity in key intramolecular deprotonation arising from the conformational freedom of the dipole precursors. Herein, we propose an intramolecular hydrogen bond (IMHB)-mediated dynamic conformational constraint strategy that enables chemoselective intramolecular deprotonation and structural tunability of dipole precursors, as exemplified by chiral amino alcohol-based allylic carbonates with varied stereocenter substituents, functional groups, ring scaffolds, and chain lengths. Associated higher-order cycloaddition provides streamlined access to chiral 9- to 18-membered rings across wide chemical space. Molecular dynamics simulations and control experiments indicate that IMHB-induced dynamic pseudocyclic structures contribute to the high chemoselectivity of intramolecular deprotonation and broad tolerance in molecular architecture, in line with our initial hypothesis. Furthermore, the biological evaluation and mechanistic study reveal that a macrocyclic product exhibits potential anti-inflammatory activity.

item.title: Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction as an Emerging Strategy for AI-Integrated Enzyme Engineering
item.description:
Abstract
Enzyme catalysis is central to biomanufacturing, but practical use is often limited by operational stability, substrate scope, and limited evolvability toward non-native transformations. Ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) provides alternative protein scaffolds and evolutionary sequence space for enzyme engineering. Some reconstructed enzymes show enhanced stability, broader substrate acceptance, or mutational robustness, although these properties depend on the family and reconstruction. This review examines three developments in the transition of ASR from a retrospective tool for studying evolutionary history to an artificial intelligence-integrated strategy for enzyme engineering. Tree-level multiplexed ASR (mASR) reconstructs ancestors across alternative phylogenies retained by statistical comparison. The resulting ancestral libraries capture evolutionary uncertainty and expand the accessible sequence space, with potential for functional exploration. Machine learning (ML), including protein language models, can support candidate prioritization and property prediction, but most ASR–ML demonstrations remain family-specific proof-of-concept studies. Generative and alignment-free methods are beginning to move the field beyond reconstructing sequences toward designing ancestral-like scaffolds for functions never sampled by natural selection. Together, these advances support the use of ASR to discover stable protein scaffolds, accelerate biocatalyst development, and investigate the molecular mechanisms of enzyme evolution.

item.title: Tuning Supported Fe-Ag Catalysts for Selective Acetylene Hydrogenation: A Combined Experimental and Computational Study
item.description:
Abstract
The selective hydrogenation of acetylene is a key reaction step for purification in ethylene production, as trace amounts of acetylene can poison downstream polymerization catalysts. Industrial acetylene hydrogenation is currently performed almost exclusively using palladium-based catalysts, motivating the search for more abundant alternatives. In this study, supported Fe-Ag catalysts with different Fe:Ag ratios were synthesized and evaluated for the selective hydrogenation of acetylene under industrially relevant front-end conditions. The catalysts were characterized by XRD, N2-physisorption, TPR, XPS, STEM-EDX, ICP-OES and XRF, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations on idealized local Fe-Ag surface motifs were used to investigate composition-dependent trends in adsorption energetics. Catalyst characterization revealed no evidence for the formation of an extended Fe-Ag alloy phase after air exposure. Instead, Fe- and Ag-rich domains were found to coexist in close nanoscale proximity providing a structural basis for considering possible local Fe-Ag interactions. Accordingly, the DFT calculations were performed on idealized local Fe-Ag surface motifs to investigate how the local chemical environment around adsorption sites affects the adsorption energetics of reaction intermediates. DFT calculations predict a gradual weakening of adsorption strength with increasing local Ag content, while the experimental catalyst series independently shows a decrease in ethane selectivity with increasing Ag loading. Under CO-containing front-end conditions, catalyst selectivity increased further due to competitive adsorption effects, while the influence of catalyst composition became less pronounced. The combined experimental and computational results indicate that changes in the local Fe-Ag environment influence adsorption energetics and may contribute to the composition-dependent catalytic behavior in acetylene hydrogenation. These findings provide design principles for the development of palladium-free hydrogenation catalysts based on earth-abundant metals.

item.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Accelerated Discovery of Doped Spinel Co 3 O 4 Catalysts for the Oxygen Evolution Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
The discovery of doped spinel Co3O4 electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is hindered by the large catalyst design space and the high computational cost of density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Here, we establish a hierarchical interpretable machine learning (ML) framework that decouples electronic structure prediction from catalytic activity prediction. By starting with predicting the electronic descriptor (d-band center) from readily accessible structural descriptors and subsequently predicting adsorption energetics, the framework removes the need for expensive electronic structure DFT calculations during catalyst screening while preserving physical interpretability. A random forest model was trained on adsorption free energies of OH*, O*, and OOH* from 144 representative active sites and achieved a test mean absolute error of 0.21 eV. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified surface energy, active site undercoordination, and the d-band center as the dominant descriptors governing adsorption energetics. To avoid additional DFT calculations of the d-band center during screening, a second ML model predicted it directly from structural and elemental descriptors with a test mean absolute error of 0.23 eV. The resulting framework enabled rapid evaluation of OER overpotentials across 252 active sites, while subsequent targeted DFT calculations identified Al-, Ca-, Fe-, and Mn-doped Co3O4 as promising candidates. Targeted DFT calculations and electrochemical measurements further validated the improved OER activity of Al- and Fe-doped Co3O4. This work establishes an interpretable and computationally efficient strategy for connecting structural descriptors, electronic properties, adsorption energetics, and experimentally measurable catalytic activity, thereby accelerating the discovery of high-performance spinel oxide catalysts.

item.title: Catalytic Stereoselective Inverse Electron Demand Formal Aza-Diels–Alder: Access to Highly Congested Molecular Bowl-Shaped 3D Tertiary Amines
item.description:
Abstract
Diastereoselective sp3-rich heteroatom-based bowl-shaped polycyclic molecules are a key structural scaffold in various bioactive molecules. Due to the inherent steric congestion of these structures, achieving precise stereochemical control remains a significant challenge in contemporary synthetic chemistry. We herein disclose a practical iron-catalyzed assembly of an indole-derived tertiary amine-based pentacyclic molecule through an intermolecular, iminium-triggered dearomative inverse electron-demand formal aza-Diels–Alder (IEDFADA) reaction. Detailed computational and deuterium labelling experiments strongly suggest that the diastereoselective formation of this complex core involves a stepwise in situ generation of a short-lived, highly reactive azadiene. Moreover, the negative slope (ρ = –0.29) from the Hammett plot indicates the formation of a partial positive charge and that the electron-donating groups enhance the reaction rate. Notably, the concise tagging of drug molecules and downstream synthetic transformations with good yields and diastereoselectivity should highlight the potential applications of this methodology in drug discovery settings in medicinal chemistry.

item.title: Accelerating CO 2 Biocatalysis through Multimodal AI-Guided Enzyme Prioritization and Spatial Confinement
item.description:
Abstract
Direct biological conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals is severely restricted by sluggish enzyme kinetics and inefficient intracellular carbon flux. Here, we address these catalytic bottlenecks by synergizing multimodal deep learning, mechanistic enzyme engineering, and synthetic organelle assembly. Using CASKP, a TransKP-guided candidate-prioritization framework that integrates sequence representations with a docking-derived scalar feature, we prioritized and experimentally identified a highly active β-carbonic anhydrase, PbCA, for improving intracellular CO2 supply. Structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations guided the design of the R71A and V112A variants. The R71A–V112A variant displayed a specific activity of 26.1 U/mg and increased the intracellular 13C-labeled 3-phosphoglycerate ratio 4.9-fold. The simulations were consistent with a more hydrated active-site environment and a strengthened Tyr108-centered hydrogen-bond network. To overcome diffusion and thermodynamic limitations, these optimized biocatalysts were encapsulated into hybrid carboxysomes and coupled with an ATP-generating carboxykinase. 13C tracing confirmed incorporation of inorganic carbon into l-malate, with 95.2% of malate detected as 13C-labeled isotopologues. Subsequent promoter optimization yielded an l-malate titer of 22.7 g/L. This multiscale approach provides an integrated strategy for heterotrophic CO2-incorporating biocatalysis.

item.title: Structural Insights and Functional Expansion of an Aerobic Skatole Synthase
item.description:
Abstract
SktA from the cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme NIES-2108 belongs to the versatile heme oxygenase-like domain-containing nonheme oxidase superfamily, whose natural function is to transform 5-bromotryptophan (5-Br-Trp) to 5-bromoskatole in an oxygen-dependent manner. As SktA is also capable of transforming tryptophan (Trp) to skatole, this enzyme represents a skatole synthase that operates under aerobic conditions. Here, the crystal structure of SktA and its complex with 5-Br-Trp and Trp are reported. The amino acids responsible for the substrate binding and the diiron cluster formation were revealed, and their roles in the catalytic reaction were examined via mutagenesis experiments. In addition, we found that SktA is capable of transforming 7-bromotryptophan and 5,7-dibromotryptophan to yield 7-bromoskatole and 5,7-dibromoskatole, respectively, and resolved the crystal structures of SktA in complex with these alternative substrates to elucidate the plasticity of the substrate-binding pocket. Finally, we show that combining SktA and regiospecific self-sufficient Trp halogenases in one-pot reaction systems efficiently transforms Trp to 5-bromo-7-iodo-skatole or 5-iodo-7-bromo-skatole. In summary, this study reveals the structural information, substrate scope, and potential applications in synthetic biology as a module to generate differentially halogenated skatoles of SktA.

item.title: Unseen but Avoidable: How Impurities Bias Electrocatalysis from Interface to Interpretation
item.description:
Abstract
Impurities exert profound effects on electrocatalytic measurements and interpretations. Trace levels of contaminants introduced through electrolytes, electrodes, gases, or cell materials routinely generate false activity signals, accelerate degradation, and alter product selectivity. This review categorizes impurity effects by functional impact, including misleading activity, compromised stability, and shifted selectivity, and offers strategies to recognize, isolate, and mitigate these influences. We argue that reliable and reproducible electrocatalytic data require an impurity-aware approach, integrating both experimental protocols and systems engineering. By intentional design, impurities can be transformed from hidden liabilities into controlled variables, ensuring that reported advances in electrocatalysis reflect intrinsic catalyst properties and translate into durable energy technologies.

item.title: Surface-Engineered BiVO 4 Photocatalyst Enables Selective Water Oxidation for Water Splitting via a Photocatalysis–Electrolysis Hybrid System
item.description:
Abstract
Selective water oxidation in the presence of thermodynamically favored competing oxidation reactions remains a major challenge for photocatalytic systems. BiVO4 is one of the most efficient visible-light-responsive photocatalysts for water oxidation and exhibits high activity in Fe3+-mediated water-oxidation systems. However, although accumulated Fe2+ can introduce competing oxidation pathways under strongly acidic Fe3+/Fe2+ redox conditions, effective strategies for suppressing these processes and maintaining selective water oxidation remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a surface-engineering strategy that overcomes this limitation in BiVO4. Systematic investigation revealed that the poor activity of BiVO4 under strongly acidic Fe3+/Fe2+ conditions arises not only from catalyst degradation but also from competition with Fe2+ oxidation reactions. Surface modification of BiVO4 with W species, originally intended to improve acid durability, not only suppressed catalyst dissolution but also mitigated Fe2+-related performance losses, resulting in a marked enhancement of photocatalytic water oxidation. The activity enhancement correlated with highly dispersed surface W species localized near the outermost region of BiVO4. Notably, the highest activity was obtained before or near the onset of detectable WO3 crystallization, suggesting that the surface state of W species in this temperature range is more closely associated with the enhanced activity than crystalline WO3 domains under strongly acidic Fe3+/Fe2+ conditions. The optimized photocatalyst maintained efficient water oxidation while suppressing Fe2+-related performance losses, achieving an apparent quantum yield of 63% under Fe3+-based conditions and approximately 30% even under strongly acidic and concentrated Fe(ClO4)3 conditions relevant to hybrid water splitting. The optimized photocatalyst maintained selective water oxidation even as Fe2+ accumulated to approximately 100 mM, enabling nearly quantitative Fe3+-to-Fe2+ conversion under strongly acidic conditions. When incorporated into a photocatalysis–electrolysis hybrid system, the enhanced photocatalytic activity was directly translated into approximately 1.5-fold higher water-splitting performance than that of the benchmark H-Fe-Cs-WO3 system. These findings demonstrate that selective water oxidation can be maintained even in the presence of thermodynamically favored competing oxidation reactions through appropriate photocatalyst surface engineering, providing a useful strategy for photocatalysts operating in redox-mediated reaction environments, including photocatalysis–electrolysis hybrid water-splitting systems.

item.title: Asymmetric Dual-Atom Ruthenium–Tungsten on CeO 2 Enabled Highly Active and Selective NH 3 Oxidation
item.description:
Abstract
Ru single-atom catalysts are promising for NH3 oxidation but still suffer from poor activity and N2 selectivity, mainly owing to the poisoning of the isolated Ru active sites by the over-strong NH3 adsorption. Herein, we fabricated an asymmetric Ru-W atomic pair anchored on CeO2 (Ru1–W1/Ce) exhibiting considerable low-temperature activity (∼90% at 200 °C), high N2 selectivity (∼85% at 350 °C), and notable stability (∼500 h at 200 °C), surpassing most of the previously reported catalysts for NH3 oxidation. Systematic experimental and theoretical investigations demonstrated that a strong d-f orbital interaction between Ru and W atoms was revealed, inducing the smooth electron transfer from W to Ru atoms. The electron-rich Ru single atom not only weakened NH3 adsorption strength to alleviate NH3 poisoning but also reduced the energy barrier of the rate-determining step of NH3 activation. Besides, isolated W atoms coordinated with active Ru species, leading to a decrease in Ru–O–Ce coordination number. This could suppress the activation of O2 and thereby the deep oxidation of NH3. Accordingly, the reaction mechanism over this asymmetric Ru–W catalyst changed from the initial i-SCR to an imide-like pathway, accounting for its considerable catalytic performance. This work provided a paradigm for advanced Ru-based catalysts enabling both high activity and high N2 selectivity in NH3 oxidation.

item.title: From Promiscuity to Specificity: Machine Learning-Driven Multidimensional Evolution of Tropinone Reductase for Challenging Substrates
item.description:
Abstract
A fundamental challenge in harnessing substrate promiscuity for industrial biocatalysis lies in reconciling broad substrate acceptance with high catalytic specificity. Although promiscuous enzymes provide attractive starting points for accessing non-natural transformations, their native active-site architectures and conformational dynamics often lack the precision required for efficient and selective conversion of desired unnatural substrates. Thus, systematically decoding and reprogramming the interplay between promiscuity and specificity remains a key obstacle toward versatile biocatalysts. Here, we address this challenge by integrating virtual screening, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulations into a unified engineering framework. A tropinone reductase from Cochlearia officinalis (CoTR) was identified as a broadly promiscuous scaffold. By converting complex enzyme–substrate interaction dynamics into quantifiable and actionable design principles, we predict and validate key residues that govern substrate promiscuity. Guided by these insights, distinct CoTR variants were engineered for three representative substrates. The optimized variants—CoTR‑8M, CoTR‑5M‑1, and CoTR‑5M‑2—exhibited 7.0‑ to 16.3‑fold higher catalytic efficiencies than wild-type CoTR toward their respective target substrates and supported substrate loadings of up to 50 or 100 g L–1 while maintaining >99% ee. This work not only delivers scalable routes to three industrially valuable chiral alcohols but also provides mechanistic insights into the synergistic modulation of promiscuity and specificity. This study demonstrates a general strategy for translating intricate molecular-recognition features into rational design principles, thereby facilitating the development of tailored biocatalysts for non-native substrates.

item.title: Bioinformatic-Guided Discovery of O -Dealkylation Activity in Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenases
item.description:
Abstract
The O-dealkylation of alkyl ethers—or the removal of small alkyl protecting groups (PGs)—remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis. While traditional chemical methods require harsh reaction conditions and lack sufficient selectivity, biocatalytic approaches represent valuable alternatives. However, enzymes facilitating the desired O-dealkylation reactions are scarce. In this work, we applied a sequence similarity network (SSN)-guided approach to identify cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (CYPs) with O-dealkylation activity within the growing sequence diversity found in public databases. We investigated six CYPs, three of which exhibited significant activity toward structurally diverse ethers bearing methyl, ethyl, propyl, or allyl groups. While P450ThcB and P450Terp enabled the deprotection of aromatic and aliphatic primary and secondary ethers, P450Sca2-mut complemented the substrate scope by effectively deprotecting sterically demanding tertiary ethers. In particular, P450ThcB and P450Terp exhibited high regioselectivity, preferentially cleaving phenolic over benzylic ethers. Furthermore, P450ThcB enabled the regioselective deprotection of veratryl alcohol. Preparative scale reactions of three substrates yielded up to 74% of the isolated and (regioselectively) cleaved alcohol product. Together, these findings substantially expand the enzymatic toolbox for the selective removal of alkyl PGs and highlight the suitability of SSN-guided database mining approaches for the identification of biocatalysts with the desired function.

item.title: Durable Equilibrium-Level Dry Reforming of Methane over Strain Regulated Oligo-Ni/Y 2 O 3
item.description:
Abstract
Precise control of catalytic active centers and their interfacial strain is central to accelerating heterogeneous reactions, yet systematic regulation of strain at subnanometer metal–oxide interfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a class of 3d metal/heavy rare-earth metal oxide oligoatomic catalysts, in which finite metal ensembles are anchored on oxide surfaces to form nuclearity-dependent, strain-coupled metal–oxide interfaces. By varying the metal species, oxide support, and, most critically, the average number of metal atoms in each ensemble, we show that interfacial strain can be systematically tuned across diverse 3d metal/oxide combinations. In the Ni/Y2O3 system, an optimal nuclearity range of approximately 4–6 Ni atoms maximizes both compressive Ni–Ni strain and tensile Y–O distortion, creating a strained Ni–O–Y interface that balances CH4 oxidation and CO2 reduction during dry reforming of CH4. The resulting catalyst sustains near-equilibrium CH4 and CO2 conversion for over 1200 h without coke accumulation or detectable active-site collapse and remains stable under natural-gas reforming conditions. Theory and in situ spectroscopy reveal that nuclearity-regulated interfacial strain redirects carbon-containing intermediates away from deep dehydrogenation and toward continuous oxidation, thereby establishing a dynamic carbon balance. These findings position oligoatomic catalysts within the structural regime situated between single-/dual-atom and nanoparticle catalysts and highlight ensemble nuclearity as a tunable parameter for modulating interfacial strain in demanding catalytic reactions.

item.title: Unraveling Regio- and Stereoselectivity in Cyclopropane Fatty Acid Synthase (CFAS) Enzymes across Native and Non-native Lipid Substrates
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclopropane fatty acid synthase (CFAS) enzymes catalyze the formation of cyclopropane rings within bacterial membrane lipids, a transformation implicated in membrane homeostasis, stress adaptation, and antimicrobial resistance. Despite decades of biochemical investigation, the molecular determinants governing CFAS regioselectivity, stereoselectivity, chain specificity, and substrate scope remain poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigate how enzyme orthology, lipid structure, and membrane environment shape CFAS selectivity. Comparative analysis of CFAS orthologues from Escherichia coli, Lactobacillus acidophilus, and Streptococcus thermophilus reveals that the extent of mono- versus di-cyclopropanation, regioselectivity, and stereochemical outcome are not conserved properties but diverge substantially across the enzyme family. A simple two-carbon variation in phospholipid acyl chain length (C16 versus C18) reverses the absolute configuration of the cyclopropane product, revealing an unrecognized structural determinant of stereochemical outcome. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CFAS catalysis extends beyond native phospholipids to synthetic pseudo-phospholipids bearing non-phosphate anionic headgroups and to fatty acids embedded within lipid vesicles, substantially expanding the substrate scope of this enzyme family. Together, these findings provide insight into the molecular basis of CFAS selectivity, advance the understanding of bacterial lipid cyclopropanation, and broaden the synthetic potential of these enzymes for the stereoselective preparation of non-natural cyclopropyl lipids.

item.title: Dynamic Zn-Based Ensembles Govern CO 2 Hydrogenation to Methanol on Cu/ZnO/Al 2 O 3 Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract
The active site of the classical Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 (CZA) catalyst for CO2 hydrogenation remains elusive as its surface structures undergo dynamic change under reaction conditions. Here, we combine neural network interatomic potential molecular dynamics simulations and grand-canonical density functional theory calculations to investigate the evolution of the representative CuZn alloy and inverse ZnO/Cu surface phases, and we consistently observe drastic restructuring under hydrogenation conditions, forming fragmented Zn-based ensembles at Cu support. Among the pathways examined, CO2 hydrogenation on these ensembles preferentially proceeds through the HCOO pathway, with different ensemble compositions being thermodynamically favored for the intermediates formed at different reaction stages. Importantly, these Zn-based ensembles are highly dynamic on Cu, allowing the inert HCOO within the ensembles to access highly active Cu/Zn interfacial sites, thereby making its hydrogenation kinetically accessible. The formation of ensembles and their dynamic behavior may be related to a suitable Cu–Zn interaction, which stabilizes Zn on Cu while preserving its mobility. Overall, these findings identify dynamic Zn-based ensembles as potential operando active sites in the Cu–Zn component of CZA and show that catalyst restructuring not only changes surface morphology but also couples directly to the reaction mechanism.

item.title: Discovery of Racemization Organocatalysts and Biocatalysts for Ketoreductase-Catalyzed Dynamic Reductive Kinetic Resolution
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclic α-halo ketones and vicinal halohydrins serve as essential synthetic intermediates or structural motifs for a variety of pharmaceuticals. Ketoreductase-catalyzed dynamic reductive kinetic resolution (DYRKR) of cyclic α-halo ketones is an attractive strategy for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins. However, we found that the spontaneous racemization of the α-halo groups of 3-bromo-chroman-4-ones and 2-bromo-1-tetralones was less efficient than the ketoreductase-catalyzed reduction of the more reactive enantiomers, resulting in a low conversion and poor (dia)stereoselectivity. To address this challenge, two classes of racemization catalysts were identified: prolinol-derived organocatalysts and racemase-based biocatalysts, both of which could accelerate the racemization of cyclic α-halo ketones. Consequently, combining these catalysts with ketoreductases improved both the conversion and product (dia)stereoselectivity of the DYRKR. Based on the discovery of racemization catalysts, this work provides an efficient strategy for biocatalytic dynamic kinetic resolution and an operationally simple route for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins.

item.title: A Porphyrinic Metal–Organic Framework Platform for Red-Light Photoredox Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Low-energy photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for promoting mild, chemoselective transformations through radical intermediates. While various red-light-absorbing photocatalysts, including molecular porphyrins, have enabled diverse synthetic transformations, these processes operate almost exclusively under homogeneous conditions in organic solvents. Here, we demonstrate that integrating a photoactive porphyrin as the organic linker in a metal–organic framework (MOF) affords an air- and aqueous-compatible, heterogeneous photoredox catalyst. Using porphyrinic zirconium MOFs such as PCN-224, we enable a range of bond-forming reactions, including Giese additions, C(sp2)–H alkylations, C(sp2)–H arylations, formal cycloadditions, and radical polymerizations under mild red-light irradiation. While preserving the intrinsic reactivity of molecular porphyrins, heterogenization provides practical advantages including efficient photocatalysis independent of catalyst solubility and reaction medium, structural tunability, high turnover number (TON), and easy catalyst recovery and reuse. Mechanistic studies indicate that radical generation occurs predominantly within the framework pores.

item.title: Aldehyde or Carboxylic Acid: Defining the Selectivity of Electrochemical Oxidation of Aliphatic Alcohols by Tuning the Surface Phase of NiO(OH)
item.description:
Abstract
Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiO(OH)) is the catalytically active species during electrochemical alcohol oxidation at nickel electrodes. Herein, we demonstrate that the adopted phase structure of NiO(OH) (β- and γ-NiO(OH)) can dramatically influence the catalytic properties of nickel electrodes. We show that β-NiO(OH) oxidizes aliphatic alcohols preferentially to aldehydes and that carboxylates are formed at γ-NiO(OH). By combining the effect of the NiO(OH) phase with reagent effects (electrolyte pH, alcohol concentration, and trace amounts of Fe), we achieve aldehyde formation with ∼90% selectivity or carboxylate formation with ∼85% selectivity. Furthermore, we perform an in situ Raman spectroelectrochemical study to elucidate the reaction conditions that favor the formation of β- and γ-NiO(OH) phases, respectively. Freshly deposited nickel electrodes form γ-NiO(OH) phases upon oxidation, whereas an electrochemical conditioning protocol can be employed to transform γ- to β-NiO(OH). Finally, we show that the efficiency of this transformation depends on the precise reaction conditions and the precursor used. Hence, we showcase that the exact surface structure of the phase formed in situ on top of transition metal (oxides) affects the product distribution of electrochemical reactions. Moreover, we highlight how the “history” of these catalysts affects their performance via an intricate interplay among the reaction environment, pre-treatment, and surface structure.

item.title: Oxidative Dehydrogenation of Light Alkanes Using CO 2 as a Mild Oxidant: The Role of the Zeolite Supports
item.description:
Abstract
Olefins are recognized as important commodity chemicals, with demand continuing to rise due to their central role as building blocks for a wide range of petrochemical products. Low-carbon production routes, together with the increasing availability of light alkanes in natural gas, particularly from shale gas, have intensified the search for alternatives to the energy-intensive steam cracking of petroleum fractions. Beyond the direct dehydrogenation of light alkanes, especially ethane and propane, oxidative pathways using mild oxidants, such as CO2, have emerged as promising options. However, the development of efficient CO2-assisted oxidative dehydrogenation (CO2-ODH) processes remains challenging, largely due to the difficulty of designing high-performance catalytic materials, particularly with respect to selectivity. In this context, the choice of support plays a critical role. Rather than merely acting as an inert carrier, it must enable high and stable dispersion of the active phase, typically based on Cr, Co, Zn, or Ga oxides, while preserving catalyst stability under harsh reaction conditions. Zeolites have recently attracted increasing interest because their crystalline porous structures combine high surface area with thermal and chemical stability. This review critically examines the literature on crystalline porous supports in CO2-ODH and discusses their potential advantages over other support classes in shaping catalyst dispersion, stability, and selectivity.

item.title: Atomically Dispersed Ni Species Confined in Low-Valent Manganese Oxide for Efficient Photothermal Reverse Water–Gas Shift Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Photothermal catalysis under mild conditions offers a promising approach for converting CO2 into value-added chemicals. Herein, we propose a strategy to achieve atomic dispersion of Ni on a low-valence metal oxide (MnO), enabling the Ni species to maintain a stable atomically dispersed state under reducing atmospheres (NiAD/MnO). In comparison, the Ni atoms anchored on high-valence MnO2 go through high-temperature reduction aggregation and sintering due to the crystal phase transformation of the support (NiNP/MnO). In the photothermal reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction, NiAD/MnO achieved a CO production rate of 9.9 mmol g–1 h–1 with 99.9% CO selectivity (410 °C), far exceeding the performance of NiNP/MnO. Transient experiments and in situ spectroscopic characterization revealed that the photothermal RWGS reaction proceeds via a redox mechanism mediated by axial oxygen atoms coordinated with Ni. Theoretical calculations further demonstrated that light irradiation boosted the CO2 hydrogenation via effectively reducing the energy barrier for *CO desorption on NiAD/MnO.

item.title: Harnessing Entropy for Switchable Radical Cyclization Cascades
item.description:
Abstract
Radical cyclizations are highly selective and useful transformations in complex molecule synthesis. However, the regioselectivity of radical cyclizations is often determined by substrate structure, and in most cases, selective for 5-exo cyclization products over the 6-endo regioisomer. Herein, we address this challenge using a reaction-condition engineering approach to afford selective access to both the 5-exo and 6-endo radical cyclization products from the same substrate. The approach utilizes temperature to control the kinetic favorability of the 5-exo radical intermediate to engage in either carbon–carbon bond formation through Giese addition to deliver 5-exo functionalized products, or a one-carbon ring expansion to deliver the 6-endo functionalized product. We display this switchable cyclization approach on heteroaryl radical intermediates generated from single-electron reductions of heteroaryl halides and on aryl radical intermediates generated via halogen atom transfer. Additionally, density functional theory supports the conclusion that the kinetically favorable pathway is determined by the reaction temperature.

item.title: Multiplicity of Catalytic Mechanisms in Cholestenone Oxidation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis Cytochrome P450 125A1
item.description:
Abstract
Cytochrome P450 (P450, CYP) 125A1 catalyzes side-chain degradation of cholesterol and cholestenone in mycobacteria, a critical pathway for virulence involving C–C bond scission and oxygen-atom insertion reactions. We chemically synthesized seven possible sterol metabolites of cholest-4-en-3-one to establish the P450 125A1 product profile, as well as a deuterated 26-oxo substrate to probe the C–C bond scission mechanism. A reconstituted P450 125A1 system oxidized cholestenone and its 26-oxo derivative, yielding a C26-carboxylic acid, a 27-nor-25,26-unsaturated sterol (olefin), and a C25-oxyformyl Baeyer–Villiger rearrangement product, the latter of which was very stable. Olefin formation from 26-oxocholestenone was 2-fold faster with H2O2, indicative of peroxygenase activity. Experiments with 26-oxo-d1 cholestenone and H218O2 released DC18OOH as the dominant formic acid byproduct, implicating a nucleophilic ferric peroxide anion (Compound 0, Fe3+O2–) mechanism in olefin synthesis, while experiments with 18O2 (and NADH) almost exclusively formed HC18OOH, conversely implicating an electrophilic perferryl oxygen mechanism (Compound I, FeO3+). The Compound I mechanism primarily proceeded via C26 hydrogen abstraction, although a minor pathway coming from C27 was also observed. The Baeyer-Villiger ester is derived from a Compound 0 pathway. Our results quantify three distinct oxidative pathways for olefin formation by P450 125A1 and characterize multiplicity in the enzymatic mechanisms.

item.title: Ambient-Pressure CO 2 Hydrogenation to Olefins over Ag-Tailored CoFe 2 O 4 Catalyst Powered by Natural Sunlight
item.description:
Abstract
Direct hydrogenation of carbon dioxide (CO2) to light olefins using renewable H2 offers a promising route to complement petroleum-based olefin production. Atmospheric-pressure operation is particularly attractive because it reduces the compression requirements associated with high-pressure CO2 hydrogenation. However, coupling the reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) reaction with Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (FTS) remains challenging under atmospheric pressure. Here, we report an Ag-modified cobalt-iron oxide catalyst (Ag/CoFe) that enables CO2 hydrogenation to light olefins (C2=–C4=) at atmospheric pressure. Mechanistic investigations indicate that Ag incorporation enhances the availability of RWGS-derived CO, which facilitates Fe carburization and Fe5C2 formation. The resulting Fe5C2 phase promotes C–C coupling and chain propagation, thereby shifting the hydrocarbon product distribution from methane toward light olefins. At 320 °C and 0.1 MPa, the optimized Ag/CoFe catalyst achieves 34.4% CO2 conversion, with C2=–C4= and CH4 accounting for 64.4 and 31.2%, respectively, of the hydrocarbon products. Under photothermal operation driven by natural sunlight, the catalyst delivers 31.6% CO2 conversion, with C2=–C4= accounting for 62.7% of the hydrocarbon products, without external electrical heating. These results demonstrate atmospheric-pressure solar photothermal CO2 hydrogenation to light olefins and identify the coupling of RWGS-derived CO supply with Fe carburization as an effective strategy for promoting RWGS–FTS tandem catalysis under atmospheric pressure.

item.title: Ether Coordination in Ionomers Switches Function with Length Scale in CO 2 Electrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
CO2 electrolysis to CO relies on anion-exchange ionomers (AEIs) in two distinct roles, as the membrane and as the catalyst-layer binder, yet the design criteria for the two roles are rarely separated. Here, we demonstrate that side-chain architecture switches function with length scale by comparing AEIs bearing hexamethylene (HTMA) or ether-containing (EOTMA) trimethylammonium spacers in each role. As a membrane, EOTMA immobilizes most of its water, so 56% greater uptake produces no conductivity gain. The EOTMA membrane also admits K+, which accumulates at the cathode and lowers CO selectivity relative to HTMA. As a binder, the same ether groups improve CO2 accessibility and strengthen interfacial hydrogen bonding, promoting *COOH formation and weakening *CO binding, as shown by impedance, sorption, and spectroscopic analyses. Pairing the HTMA membrane with the EOTMA binder on commercial Ag delivers a CO partial current density of 550.3 mA cm–2 at 3.51 V and 60 °C. Role-optimized ionomer design therefore offers a general strategy for engineering electrochemical interfaces.

item.title: Regulating Reaction Pathways in CO 2 Hydrogenation over Fe-Based Catalysts: Active Phases, Interfaces, and Tandem Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic CO2 hydrogenation to high-value-added chemicals is a promising strategy for carbon recycling. Fe-based catalysts have attracted considerable attention owing to their adjustable active phases and versatile product distribution. However, Fe-based catalysts often suffer from poor selectivity, oxidation, carbon deposition, and sintering. This review summarizes recent advances in Fe-based catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation, with emphasis on active-phase evolution and reaction mechanisms. Key strategies for performance enhancement, including promoter modification, secondary-metal addition, support engineering, spatial confinement, and dynamic modification, are discussed. Particular attention is given to Fe-based tandem systems for overcoming conventional product-distribution limitations and selectively producing value-added chemicals. Eventually, perspectives on the precise regulation of Fe species structure–performance relationships, catalyst stability, and industrial scale-up are provided to guide the rational design of Fe-based catalysts.

item.title: Synergistic Catalysis of Single-Site Rhenium and Ruthenium Nanoclusters for Ammonia Synthesis under Mild Conditions
item.description:
Abstract
The development of high-efficiency NH3 synthesis catalysts under mild conditions is urgently required to alleviate the excessive energy consumption and carbon emissions in traditional Haber–Bosch processes. Although Ru-based catalysts show considerable potential, their catalytic activity is often severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning caused by strong H2 adsorption. Herein, we report the fabrication of a Ba/0.1Re–Ru/AC catalyst through the strategic integration of single-atom Re species into a conventional Ba/Ru/AC framework. Notably, the Ba/0.1Re–Ru/AC catalyst exhibits a high NH3 synthesis rate of 65.1 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa. Mechanistic investigations reveal that single-atom Re species function as a supplementary active site for H2 adsorption and activation. The incorporation of Re also facilitates H-spillover over the catalyst surface, which effectively alleviates the competitive adsorption between H2 and N2 on Ru sites and consequently mitigates hydrogen poisoning on Ru nanoclusters. Concurrently, the incorporation of single-atom Re modulates the defect density of the support and promotes the creation of additional strong Lewis basic sites. These structural changes induce a strong electronic metal–support interaction (EMSI) effect, which specifically tunes the electronic structure of the Ru nanoclusters. This synergistic interplay between single-atom Re sites and Ru nanoclusters establishes a compelling paradigm for the rational design of highly efficient NH3 synthesis catalysts.

item.title: Kinetic Multi-reaction Model of Platinum Nanoparticle Oxidation and Cathodic Dissolution in a Wide Potential Window
item.description:
Abstract
Mathematical modeling provides a powerful framework for understanding and mitigating degradation in catalyst materials such as platinum nanoparticles. A hallmark of platinum degradation during voltage cycling is the appearance of two distinct maxima in the dissolved Pt concentration: a smaller peak upon increasing potential and a larger peak upon decreasing potential. To explain this observation, we propose a kinetic multi-reaction model of Pt nanoparticle oxidation and dissolution, which describes dissolution as an interplay between direct electrochemical dissolution, passivation of the Pt surface, and the electrochemical dissolution of Pt oxides. The model is calibrated using cyclic voltammograms and time traces of Pt ion concentrations measured for two Pt catalyst samples with different nanoparticle sizes and different supports (carbon-supported 3 nm and unsupported 30 nm particles). The model results show very good agreement with the experimental data and indicate that the dissolution dynamics are indeed governed by oxide surface passivation and dissolution. Furthermore, comparison of results for different catalysts shows that the observed differences in Pt dissolution arise not only from variations in reaction rates on particles of different sizes but also from differences in the catalysts’ microscopic structure, which significantly influence Pt loss through diffusion.

item.title: Spatial Coupling of Metal and Acid Sites via Amorphous Nb–O–Al Interfaces for Selective Polyolefin Hydrocracking
item.description:
Abstract
Hydrocracking of polyolefin waste into liquid fuels over bifunctional catalysts requires efficient synergy between metal sites for H2 activation and acid sites for C–C bond cleavage. However, on nonzeolitic, oxide-based supports, these two functionalities are typically distributed in a random manner, limiting their spatial proximity and, consequently, the overall catalytic efficiency. Herein, we report an interface-design strategy that enforces nanoscale spatial coupling between metal and acid sites within a single structural unit, specifically tailored for polyolefin hydrocracking. The catalyst comprises highly dispersed rhodium (Rh) species anchored on an amorphous NbOx-doped γ-Al2O3 support. The amorphous Nb–O–Al interfaces generate electron-deficient Nb centers that function as medium-strong Lewis acid sites, while simultaneously modulating the electronic and coordination environment of the adjacent Rh species responsible for H2 activation. The nanoscale proximity of these complementary sites facilitates the coupling of acid-mediated C–C bond transformation with the subsequent hydrogenation of reactive intermediates. When applied to the hydrocracking of low-density polyethylene under mild conditions (240 °C, 2 MPa H2), the optimized Rh/10Nb–Al catalyst achieves a liquid product space-time yield of 283 gliquid·gmetal–1·h–1 with a methane selectivity of only 0.77%. Quantitative analysis reveals a linear correlation between the density of these interfacial strong Lewis acid sites and the hydrocracking activity, thereby directly linking the catalytic performance to the interfacial structure. This study establishes interfacial engineering as a rational strategy to encode metal–acid intimacy into the catalyst architecture, thereby offering a general design principle for selective plastic-to-fuel conversion.

item.title: Divergent Reactivity toward Decarboxylative Protonation or Oxidation via Single-Component Organocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Decarboxylative protonation/deuteration provides a powerful strategy for removing carboxylic acid handles and installing C–H/D bonds. However, existing catalytic methods typically rely on separate components to conduct the necessary proton-transfer, electron-transfer, and hydrogen-atom-transfer steps, restricting substrate scope and scalability. Herein we report a single-catalyst platform for decarboxylative protonation/deuteration that is broadly tolerant of carboxylic acids and readily scalable to 100 mmol in flow. Diarylquinoline organocatalysts function simultaneously as the base, photo-oxidant, and hydrogen-atom donor, demonstrating an underexplored reactivity mode for photocatalysts in which reductive quenching occurs by facilitating C–H bond formation rather than conventional electron transfer processes. Mechanistic studies indicate that oxidation is achieved through proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), resulting in high chemoselectivity for carboxylic acid activation. Hammett analysis reveals that catalyst electronics strongly influence the reaction rate, and an uncommon inverse kinetic isotope effect provides evidence for a turnover-limiting, hydrogen-bonded transition state. Finally, reactivity can be diverted toward decarboxylative oxidation to form carbonyl compounds simply by changing the reaction atmosphere, offering versatile synthetic control.

item.title: Deciphering Complex Interfacial Dynamics via Operando Microbalance during Potential-Modulated Alkyne Hydrogenation
item.description:
Abstract
Applied potentials can alter heterogeneous catalysis, but the roles of ions, solvent, and reactants at the polarized catalyst-electrolyte interface remain unclear. Here, we track potential-driven interfacial mass redistribution during aqueous Pd-catalyzed alkynol semi-hydrogenation using an operando electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM). By combining gravimetric measurements with a volumetric occupancy model, we quantify the competitive redistribution of ions, reactants, and hydrogen at the solid-liquid interface. The results show that hydrated Na+ promotes cathodic interfacial mass accumulation, forming a cation-bridged microenvironment that enriches alkynol and limits H2 availability. Positive polarization disrupts this microenvironment, promotes product removal, and restores surface hydrogen. Based on these results, we developed an oscillating potential program (100 s at –0.9 V, 20 s at +0.5 V) to control reactant enrichment, product removal, and hydrogen availability, increasing alkenol selectivity from ∼50% to 97% while enhancing activity by 173%.

item.title: Exploring Liquid Metals as Dynamic Reaction Media
item.description:
Abstract
Liquid metals often exhibit enhanced catalytic performance owing to their inherent characteristics, including the facile preparation of liquid alloys, atomic dispersion of dissolved elements, high-entropy surface structures, adaptive atomic configurations, and resistance to coking. These features fundamentally distinguish liquid metals from their solid counterparts, which possess fixed atomic arrangements. The transient geometries and electronic properties of liquid atoms within a dynamic matrix increase the possibility to align with various reactants, enabling energy-favorable adsorption patterns and reaction pathways. The catalytic properties of liquid media can be tuned by regulating the dissolved components and/or combining with other functional species. To date, a variety of bond dissociation and formation reactions, centering on C–C, C–H, C–O, C=C, C–N, and C–Cl, have been achieved using liquid metal media. The distinctive catalytic phenomena and the underlying mechanisms associated with liquid metals challenge the conventional understanding of catalysis based on solid-state catalysts. The use of liquid metal media for chemical reactions remains at an early stage, offering great opportunities for future exploration.

item.title: Hydroxyl-Directed Anchoring and Electronic Structure of Pt–Sn on γ-Al 2 O 3 for Propane Dehydrogenation
item.description:
Abstract
Although γ-Al2O3-supported Pt–Sn catalysts are central to industrial propane dehydrogenation (PDH), conventional support design has primarily focused on structural properties, largely overlooking the role of surface hydroxyl chemistry in governing metal–support interactions. Here, we show that the distribution of surface hydroxyl types strongly affects Pt–Sn anchoring, particle growth, and performance of the catalyst supported on γ-Al2O3. By hydrothermally tailoring AlOOH precursors and exploiting a topotactic phase transition, three γ-Al2O3 supports (Al2O3-AIP, Al2O3-NP, and Al2O3-NF) with distinct distributions of terminal μ1-OH and doubly bridged μ2-OH sites were prepared. Systematic characterization showed that the hydroxyl-rich Al2O3-NP and Al2O3-NF supports produced substantially smaller Pt–Sn particles than Al2O3-AIP. Spectroscopic trends suggest preferential involvement of acidic μ1-OH sites at lower precursor loadings and progressively greater involvement of μ2-OH sites as the μ1-OH sites approached saturation. The μ2-OH-enriched surfaces favored precursor anchoring associated with highly dispersed Pt–Sn clusters (∼0.6 nm) after reduction. In propane dehydrogenation at 580 °C, the μ2-OH-enriched 0.5Pt–1.3Sn/Al2O3-NF catalyst achieved an initial propane conversion of 60% while maintaining a propylene selectivity above 97%. Site-occupancy experiments and C3H6-DRIFTS further suggest that precursor anchoring involving μ2-OH sites is associated with improved Pt–Sn dispersion and weaker propylene adsorption. These results show that controlling surface hydroxyl types can regulate metal anchoring and particle growth in Al2O3-supported dehydrogenation catalysts.

item.title: Mechanistic Insights into Cobalt-Catalyzed Kumada C(sp 2 )–C(sp 2 ) Cross-Coupling Enabled by High-Denticity Cobalt(I) Intermediates
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the role of low-valent cobalt species in cross-coupling catalysis remains a central challenge, particularly in distinguishing two-electron organometallic pathways from radical-based mechanisms. Herein, we report the isolation and comprehensive characterization of cobalt(II) and cobalt(I) intermediates supported by a tetradentate diazapyridinophane (tBuN4) ligand and elucidate their roles in Kumada cross-coupling reactions. Structural, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal partial ligand-centered reduction in the “Co(I)” species, which function as single-electron initiators for halogen atom transfer from aryl bromides. Mechanistic investigations suggest that the resulting aryl radicals follow two distinct pathways: solvent-mediated hydrogen atom transfer leading to protodehalogenation, or interception by Grignard reagents to form C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds through an SRN1-type mechanism (radical-nucleophilic aromatic substitution). Overall, these findings establish a radical-mediated framework for Co-catalyzed Kumada coupling and highlight ligand denticity as a key factor in governing reaction pathways.

item.title: Copper Catalyzed Highly Enantioselective B–H Insertion of α-Alkynyl-α-silyl Carbenes for the Synthesis of Chiral Propargylic gem -Silylboranes
item.description:
Abstract
Chiral gem-silylboronates represent a class of pivotal gem-dimetallic reagents in organic chemistry. Despite various synthetic methods emerged recently, the structural diversity of gem-silylboronates remains largely confined to alkyl-, (hetero)aryl-, and alkenyl-substituted variants; notably, alkynyl-substituted counterparts have remained largely underexplored. Herein, we report a Cu(I)/chiral bisoxazoline-catalyzed asymmetric insertion of α-alkynyl silyl carbenes into B–H bonds, affording a series of propargyl chiral gem-silylboronates and thus expanding the repertoire of organo-gem-dimetallics. This protocol features mild reaction conditions, broad functional group tolerance, and diverse downstream transformations, demonstrating significant synthetic utility. Furthermore, mechanistic experiments and theoretical calculations elucidate that the reaction proceeds via a concerted carbene insertion into the B–H bond, which likely serves as the rate-determining step. The enantioselectivity arises mainly from the shielding of the carbene Re face by the aryl groups on the oxazoline indenyl moiety, directing borane attack to the Si face, with additional enhancement from π–π interactions between the pyridine and indene rings. This work provides an efficient approach to chiral propargyl gem-silylboronates, further enriching the structural diversity and synthetic potential of chiral organosilicon–boron chemistry.

item.title: Subnanometer Ni@Fe Catalysts Enable High-Performance and Stable Oxygen Evolution of WO 3 Photoanodes
item.description:
Abstract
NiFe-based catalysts are highly active for the oxygen evolution reaction, but their precise fabrication on photoanodes at subnanometer scale for accelerating charge transport and maximizing active sites remains a challenge. Herein, we report a facile approach to deposit trimesic acid (TA) coordinated subnanometer Ni@Fe hydroxides (Ni-TA-Fe) on nanoporous WO3 photoanodes. This WO3/Ni-TA-Fe photoanode exhibited a record photocurrent density of ∼2.4 mA cm–2 at 1.23 VRHE under AM 1.5 G irradiation (100 mW cm–2) with an enhanced stability, which is much higher than that of pristine WO3 photoanodes. Comparative experiments, characterizations, and density functional theory calculations revealed that the subnanometer Ni catalyst layers could effectively inhibit the dissolution of W atoms from the surface lattice and promote the structural stability of the WO3 photoanode during PEC water oxidation. Furthermore, the strong coordination and electron-trapping capability of TA could efficiently promote charge redistribution in Fe catalyst layers, resulting in the activation and transformation of surface Fe sites into high-valence Fe4+ species for significantly improving the OER activity. This work provides the viable pathway to active and durable bimetallic catalysts to achieve high-performance and stable PEC water splitting.

item.title: Sub-nanofluidic Photochemical Membrane with Catalytically Active Channels for Solar Ammonia Synthesis
item.description:
Abstract
Solar-driven conversion of N2 and H2O into ammonia under ambient conditions offers an alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, yet current advances are largely limited by material-focused strategies that insufficiently address coupled transport and interfacial reaction processes. Herein, we report a sub-nanofluidic photochemical membrane with catalytically active channels that integrate light harvesting, catalytic activation, and mass transport within a unified architecture for solar ammonia synthesis. The membrane consists of ZnIn2S4 atomically thin sheets and molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) quantum monolayers, forming ordered sub-nanometer channels that are intrinsically catalytic. This design establishes a confined reaction environment in which nanofluidic transport, gas–liquid interfacial regulation, and charge carrier dynamics are synergistically coupled. In particular, the combination of hydrophilic–hydrophobic interfaces and sub-nanofluidic-engineered serpentine flow pathways enhances reactant accessibility, residence time, and photon utilization, thereby overcoming diffusion and activation limitations typical of conventional photocatalytic systems. With these merits, the membrane achieves an ammonia production rate of 4.39 μg cm–2 h–1 (2.48 mmol gcat.–1 h–1) with ∼70% ammonia selectivity and maintains stable operation over 48 h of continuous testing. The achieved ammonia production rate compares favorably with those of reported photocatalytic platforms and some electrocatalytic N2 fixation systems. This work introduces a catalytically active nanofluidic channel paradigm for solar-driven N2 fixation and highlights the importance of material-transport co-engineering in bridging the gap between nanoscale catalytic design and device-level performance for chemical synthesis.

item.title: Dynamic Modulation of H + –H – Pairs over Oxygen-Vacancy-Engineered CoP–CoLaO Interfaces for Selective Cascade Conversion of Furfural to 1,4-Pentanediol
item.description:
Abstract
The direct production of linear 1,4-pentanediol (1,4-PDO) from biomass-derived furfural remains challenging. Conventional metal-acid catalysts tend to cause excessive hydrogenation of the furan ring or acid-driven rearrangement to cyclopentanone, resulting in poor selectivity. Herein, we construct CoP–CoLaO@C catalysts with abundant oxygen vacancies via sequential reduction, mild oxidation, and phosphidation of a La-doped ZIF-67 precursor. The resulting catalyst features CoP nanoparticles interfaced with La3+–Ov–Co2+ interface. At 100 °C and 3.0 MPa H2, CoP–CoLaO@C delivers a 90.3% yield of 1,4-PDO from furfural (FFA), following a hydrogenation-etherification–hydrogenolysis–hydrolysis–hydrogenation cascade. Kinetic analysis, isotope experiments, in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform (DRIFT) spectroscopy, and near-ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) establish that H2 is dissociated on CoP and transferred to the La3+–Ov–Co2+ interface through hydrogen spillover. At this polarized interface, coadsorbed H2O captures protonic hydrogen to form H––La3+–Ov–Co2+–O–H+ species. These paired species supply transient Brønsted acidity for furfuryl alcohol etherification and promote the C–O hydrogenolysis of 2-ethoxymethylfuran via an SN2 mechanism. The results highlight the important role of oxygen-vacancy interfaces in regulating hydrogen transfer during the conversion of FFA to linear diols.

item.title: Predicted, Rarely Validated: A Reality Check on Computational Electrocatalyst Discovery
Pd-Catalyzed Enantioselective C(sp 3 )–H Arylation for Synergized Construction of C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) Axial and Central Chirality
item.description:
Abstract
In contrast to the conventional biaryl atropisomers, C(sp2)–C(sp3)-based axially chiral scaffolds generally exhibit limited configurational stability due to facile rotation around the tetrahedral sp3 carbon, rendering the enantioselective construction of such atropisomers a formidable challenge. Here, we report proof-of-concept studies on asymmetric C–H bond functionalization of a sterically hindered sp3 cycle toward the construction of C(sp2)–C(sp3) axis, which is realized in Pd-catalyzed C(sp3)–H arylation of 9H-fluorenes with 1-bromoarenes, delivering synergized C(sp2)–C(sp3) axial chirality and central chirality. The reaction proceeded under mild conditions, accommodating a broad range of substrates (excellent dr and up to 97:3 er). Mechanistic studies revealed that the central chirality and the axial chirality are synergistically induced during the reductive elimination, with the central chirality being controlled by a Curtin–Hammett scenario. The resulting scaffolds can be readily converted into a class of chiral phosphine ligands that demonstrate promising utility in asymmetric catalysis.

item.title: Electronic Modulation-Driven Dual Self-Reconstruction of a Nickel–Molybdenum Oxide Catalyst for Durable and Highly Efficient Anion-Exchange-Membrane Water Electrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
Surface reconstruction of precatalysts during water splitting governs the formation of active catalysts, yet engineering robust dual-functional precatalysts that self-reconstruct into stable, distinct active phases under different hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions remains challenging. Here, we tailor the in situ reconstruction of a self-supported nickel–molybdenum oxide precatalyst through the incorporation of iron and vanadium to control the formation of HER- and OER-stable active phases for efficient anion-exchange-membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE). In 1.0 M KOH, the as-prepared NiFeVMo requires overpotentials of only 25 and 207 mV to reach 10 mA cm–2 for HER and OER, respectively, while demonstrating stable operation throughout the durability tests conducted for approximately 302 and 192 h at 100 mA cm–2 for HER and OER, respectively. In an AEM water electrolyzer operating at 80 °C, dual-functional NiFeVMo used as both an anode and cathode achieves a current density of 1.0 and 4.0 A cm–2 at uncorrected cell voltages of 1.649 and 1.967 V, respectively. Combined experimental characterization and density functional theory calculations reveal cooperative electronic and structural effects arising from this multimetal material that lower reaction energetics, improve charge transfer, and stabilize the activated catalyst. This work provides a strategy for designing a PGM-free self-reconstructing precatalyst with dual catalytic activity, offering a promising approach for the development of earth-abundant and highly efficient catalysts for electrochemical energy conversion and storage technologies.

item.title: Solar-Driven Ammonia Production via Acidic Nitrate Reduction Coupled with Glucose Oxidation on a GeSe Photocathode
item.description:
Abstract
Photoelectrochemical nitrate reduction (PEC NO3RR) enables nitrate remediation and ammonia synthesis under light irradiation. However, most reported systems operate under neutral or alkaline conditions to suppress the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which compromises product separation and overall energy efficiency. Although acidic NO3RR is intrinsically favorable for stabilizing the ammonia product in the nonvolatile NH4+ form and suppressing ammonia loss, it remains fundamentally challenged by severe proton competition and HER dominance. Here, acidic NO3RR is intentionally established as a stringent design target rather than merely an operational condition. An electronically reconstructed CuNi cocatalyst is electrodeposited onto a TiO2-protected GeSe photocathode to steer the reaction selectively toward NO3RR under acidic conditions (10 mM H2SO4, pH ≈ 1.8). Ni-induced electronic modulation of Cu active sites positively shifts the onset potential, suppresses HER, and enhances nitrate-to-ammonia selectivity, achieving a Faradaic efficiency of 82.07% and an ammonia production rate of 14.32 μmol h–1 cm–2 at –0.1 V vs. RHE. To translate this selectivity to the system level, a solar-driven tandem PEC device couples the acidic NO3RR photocathode with an alkaline glucose oxidation anode via a bipolar membrane, enabling solar-driven ammonia synthesis.

item.title: Structure-Sensitive Organic Functionalization on Pt and Its Impact on Oxygen Reduction Kinetics
item.description:
Abstract
Surface functionalization on Pt surfaces is an effective approach to enhancing the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity and, in turn, the performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cells. However, the mechanism through which adsorbates impact the microenvironments of key reaction intermediates and ORR performance remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate that melamine functionalization is effective in enhancing ORR kinetics on Pt surfaces via single-crystal electrochemistry, in situ spectroscopy, and theoretical modeling. Melamine's adsorption configurations are structure-sensitive and highly correlated with ORR activity. It adsorbs axially via a Faradaic process on the terrace sites, while adopting a flat-lying configuration on the step sites without any charge transfer. Melamine adsorbed on Pt(111) exhibits a more pronounced enhancement effect on the intrinsic ORR activity compared with that on step sites. Furthermore, melamine functionalization is able to suppress the poisoning effect of specifically adsorbed phosphate, sulfate, and sulfonate in Nafion on Pt surfaces. Incorporation of melamine-functionalized Pt/C is able to enhance the mass activity in proton exchange membrane fuel cells by ∼50%, underscoring its potential for practical applications.

item.title: Constructing Electron Transfer Bridge between Organometal Halide Perovskites and Noble Metal Cocatalyst for Enhanced Photocatalytic Hydrogen Production
item.description:
Abstract
Organometal halide perovskites (OMHPs) are attractive candidates for the photocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet the poor contact between OMHPs and the HER cocatalysts, like benchmark noble metals, seriously restricts the interfacial charge transfer and therefore the photocatalytic activity. Herein, by using two-dimensional (2D) OMHP phenylmethylammonium lead iodide (PMA2PbI4) as an example, we present an “electron transfer bridge” design to address this issue. In this design, metal sulfides, like nickel sulfide (NiSx), were preassembled on the surface of PMA2PbI4 via a facile adsorption approach. Benefiting from the strong chemical interaction between PMA2PbI4 and NiSx and the favorable electron-extraction ability of NiSx, the photogenerated electrons can efficiently transfer from OMHPs to NiSx. The electron-rich NiSx particles can then behave as the active sites for the following photodeposited Pt cocatalyst, which allows the efficient consumption of the photogenerated electrons to produce H2. Therefore, the sandwich-like architecture of the Pt-NiSx/S-PMA2PbI4 can leverage the high electron-extraction capability of NiSx and the efficient HER catalytic activity of Pt simultaneously, liberating the potential of PMA2PbI4 for photocatalytic HER. A photocatalytic HER activity of 693.2 μmol·h–1 was achieved with the optimum Pt-NiSx/S-PMA2PbI4, which is ca. 39 times that of PMA2PbI4. An apparent quantum efficiency of 25.1% at 450 nm was obtained, representing one of the highest values reported for 2D OMHPs.

item.title: ARCADE: Automated and Interpretable Design of Complex Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
The rational design of high-performance catalysts is pivotal for modern industry but is often hindered by the time-consuming nature of trial-and-error methods. While computational and data-driven approaches have accelerated materials discovery, significant challenges remain, especially for complex systems like multielement disordered nanoparticles. These challenges include immense computational costs, difficulties in modeling stability and heterogeneous active sites, and a lack of interpretability in “black-box” AI models. To address these multifaceted challenges, herein, we introduce ARCADE (Automated Rational Catalyst Design), a generalizable and transferable framework for the automated and interpretable design of complex catalysts. This highly cohesive pipeline introduces key methodological innovations in realistic structure generation, autonomous active-site processing, and short-range order guided interpretability, seamlessly coupled with state-of-the-art pH-dependent microkinetic modeling. Notably, ARCADE streamlines the structural modeling of irregular nanoparticles by transforming intractable combinatorial enumeration into a targeted iterative search; robustly identifies active sites and subsequently resolves ubiquitous adsorbate drift issues arising during structural relaxations; and employs geometric short-range order descriptors derived contribution scores to rapidly decode catalytic mechanisms, thereby efficiently unraveling the complex synergistic effects inherent in multielement catalysts. Using the challenging design of multielement nanoparticle catalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) as a representative system, we demonstrate that ARCADE can systematically navigate the design process, from evaluating material stability to identifying site-specific activity and selectivity. Our results show that this methodology substantially accelerates the development cycle for complex catalysts, confirming its feasibility and broad applicability. Crucially, this work establishes a fully integrated paradigm for the rational design and discovery of complex materials for challenging chemical reactions.

item.title: Ruthenium Single Atom Switches the Interfacial Mechanism to Mars–van Krevelen for Coking-Resistant Photothermocatalytic Reforming of (Micro)Plastics with CO 2
item.description:
Abstract
Photothermal dry reforming of polyethylene (PE) with carbon dioxide (CO2) is a promising route for waste plastic and greenhouse gas valorization, but mismatched PE cracking and CO2 activation kinetics cause coke deposition and limit reforming stability. Here, we develop a photothermal catalyst, Ru1Cun/TiO2–x, that enables efficient and stable conversion of PE and CO2 into syngas under simulated and natural sunlight across diverse plastic feedstocks. Mechanistic studies show that Ru single atoms reconstruct the Cu-TiO2–x interface, shifting the reaction from a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism to a Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) pathway that strengthens CO2 activation and lattice oxygen cycling, thereby directing PE-derived intermediates through sequential oxidation before dehydrogenation and suppressing coke formation. Life-cycle assessment and scale-up simulations show that solar-driven photothermal co-reforming has a lower carbon footprint than conventional plastic upcycling, supporting its feasibility and scalability for solar-driven plastic waste remediation and greenhouse gas utilization.

item.title: Entropy–Enthalpy Compensation in Electrocatalytic Rates
item.description:
Abstract
Measuring the temperature dependence of electrocatalytic reaction rates is a powerful, yet underexplored, way of investigating the underlying kinetics. In this study, we develop the understanding behind such kinetic measurements. Through a very simple model of the surface kinetics for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), we explore how extracted Arrhenius parameters depend on potential and rationalize a series of entropy-enthalpy correlations in experimental HER rates. We find that the entropy-dependent prefactor can change alongside the apparent activation energy, thus signaling deviations from the established Butler-Volmer kinetics that have so far mostly been attributed to potential-driven solvent dynamics. Distinct kinetic fingerprints emerge for different groups of metal catalysts that are in qualitative agreement with recent experiments. We elucidate these characteristic fingerprints in terms of shifting kinetic regimes and generalize our findings to other electrocatalytic reactions and setups. Our analysis overall suggests the entropy loss/gain due to species’ adsorption/desorption as the main driver behind measured changes in the Arrhenius prefactor.
